cards.title: P versus NP
cards.formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
cards.definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time \(C(n+1)^{k}\) for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
cards.why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

context_blocks.text: A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.

cards.title: Superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds
cards.formal:
Does there exist one total, length-preserving, deterministic polynomial-time function
\[F:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad |F(x)|=|x|,\]
whose unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not linear? Precisely, writing \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n}\) for its restriction to inputs of length \(n\), the requested lower bound is
\[\forall C>0\ \forall N\ge1\ \exists n\ge N:\quad \operatorname{CC}(F_n)>Cn.\]
Here \(C\) is real and \(N,n\) are integers. Preserve the card's polynomial-time meaning of “explicit” and its allowance of \(n\) output bits. The lower bound need only exceed every fixed linear bound at arbitrarily large lengths.
cards.definitions:
A binary string is a finite sequence of bits; \(\{0,1\}^{*}\) contains all such strings, including the empty string. Length preservation requires exactly \(n\) output bits on an \(n\)-bit input, and the empty output on the empty input. Polynomial-time computation means that a single deterministic multitape Turing machine, with no advice or oracle, outputs \(F(x)\) and halts on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps, for fixed constants \(a\ge1\) and integer \(d\ge1\). Writing the output counts toward the running time.

For each fixed \(n\), a competing circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with \(n\) input wires, optional free constants 0 and 1, gates computing arbitrary Boolean functions of at most two input bits, and an ordered list of \(n\) output wires. This is the full \(B_2\) basis: all two-input truth tables are allowed, including AND, OR, XOR and functions that ignore an input; unary NOT is also allowed. Each gate contributes one unit of size. Inputs, constants and output designations contribute zero. A wire may feed arbitrarily many gates or output positions, and intermediate gates may be shared by several outputs. Depth is unrestricted. An output may be an input wire, a constant or a gate output.

The circuit computes \(F_n\) exactly if its ordered output vector equals \(F_n(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). The number \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)\) is the minimum gate count of any such circuit. Competing circuits are nonuniform: the choice at each length is independent, and no algorithm is required to construct their descriptions. In contrast, the polynomial-time algorithm for \(F\) must work uniformly at all lengths. This distinction is part of the target.

The statement \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)=O(n)\) means that there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(N\ge1\) such that \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)\le Cn\) for every integer \(n\ge N\). The displayed target is its exact negation. It does not require \(\operatorname{CC}(F_n)/n\) to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. The function, its program and its running-time polynomial are chosen before all the lower-bound quantifiers.

The source uses AND, OR and NOT gates and leaves “explicit” broad. Every full-basis gate has a constant-size AND/OR/NOT implementation, and those gates are already allowed in \(B_2\). Thus changing between these two fixed bases changes minimum size by at most a constant factor and preserves the not-\(O(n)\) target. The polynomial-time explicitness convention is the previously recorded specialization of the source; it is not claimed to be equivalent to every possible meaning of “explicit.” No linearity or other algebraic restriction is imposed on \(F\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated existence claim. A positive answer must specify one total length-preserving function, prove that one uniform deterministic algorithm computes it in polynomial time, and prove the displayed lower bound against every circuit in the full model. A negative answer must show that every such polynomial-time function has \(O(n)\)-size nonuniform circuits, allowing the constant and starting length to depend on the function. A fixed constant-factor lower bound does not establish the target. Nor does a lower bound only for formulas, monotone circuits, XOR-only circuits or a fixed depth bound without a proof extending it to unrestricted circuits. The claim is unconditional, and an oracle-relative or conditional separation alone does not settle it. All complexity and quantifier requirements are exact; no numerical acceptance tolerance applies.
cards.why: A superlinear lower bound would establish a basic limitation on unrestricted nonuniform computation for an efficiently computable function. It would surpass every fixed linear gate count, even when a circuit can reuse work freely across outputs, and expose structure that simple counting does not identify.

The 2018 source formulation, Li–Yang Theorem 1.1 and basis, the 2025 cover-work introduction, the February 2026 gate-simplification abstract/introduction, and the July 2026 matrix-natural-proofs revision including Corollary 1’s proof and Corollaries 3–4 were read. context_blocks.text: A circuit may reuse any intermediate result and share it among different outputs. Those permissions make it stronger than a formula, whose computation is organized as a tree. The question retains all this circuit power and asks for an efficiently computable function that cannot be implemented with a fixed number of gates per input bit.

Counting proves that most Boolean truth tables require exponentially many gates. It does not supply a function computable by one polynomial-time algorithm, so it does not satisfy this card’s explicitness requirement. The challenge is obtaining a size lower bound for a computationally accessible function.

Linear maps over \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\), with addition modulo two, form a significant special case. An efficiently constructible binary matrix \(A_n\) defines \(F_n(x)=A_nx\). Counting gives matrices needing \(\Omega(n^2/\log n)\) gates, but the 2026 source still identifies a superlinear lower bound for explicit matrices as open. A lower bound for circuits using only XOR gates would not automatically apply to circuits with arbitrary Boolean gates.

The desired function already has polynomial-size circuits because its uniform polynomial-time computation can be simulated by circuits. The question therefore separates linear size from polynomial size within efficient computation. Such a lower bound alone is not a proof that \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). Conversely, a hard NP language need not be polynomial-time computable and so need not meet this card’s explicitness condition.

Li and Yang prove a \(3.1n-o(n)\) lower bound for suitable affine dispersers in the full two-input Boolean basis. An affine disperser is nonconstant on every affine subspace above its specified dimension threshold; suitable examples are polynomial-time computable. This is a substantial improvement of the known linear constant, while every fixed constant remains compatible with \(O(n)\) circuits.

The 2025 covering paper relates circuit lower bounds to combinatorial cover complexity and proves bounds for random graphs. Its results do not exhibit a polynomial-time function with the superlinear unrestricted circuit lower bound requested here.

The February 2026 gate-elimination preprint gives formal simplification results for selected bases and an efficiently checkable form of a classical linear parity lower bound. Its additional proof structure does not supply a superlinear unrestricted bound.

Raz’s July 2026 revision proves conditional barriers for matrix natural proofs: proofs identifying a sufficiently large set of hard matrices recognizable in time polynomial in the matrix description. Under the cryptographic assumptions stated in that paper, pseudorandom matrices with small circuits obstruct this defined proof class. The near-linear and linear circuit-size barriers rely on different assumptions; neither rules out all possible proofs of this card’s target.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\)? Equivalently, do there exist a single deterministic Turing machine \(A\) and a constant \(C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\ge1\), directed graph \(G\) on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(s,t\in[n]\), the machine halts, correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and visits at most
\[C\left\lceil\log_2(n+2)\right\rceil\]
work-tape cells? The graph is given explicitly by its adjacency matrix; the input is read-only. The machine and constant must work for all input sizes.
cards.definitions:
A directed graph has a set \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) of ordered edges. Self-loops are allowed. Reachability asks whether there are vertices \(v_0=s,\ldots,v_\ell=t\), with \(\ell\ge0\), such that \((v_{i-1},v_i)\in E\) for every \(1\le i\le\ell\). In particular \(s=t\) is a yes instance. No degree, planarity, acyclicity or unique-path restriction is imposed.

The input contains a self-delimiting binary encoding of \(n\), all \(n^2\) adjacency bits in row order, and \(s,t\) in fixed-length binary vertex fields. Its bit length is \(N=\Theta(n^2)\), so logarithmic bounds in \(N+2\) and \(n+2\) agree up to constants. Malformed strings, including invalid dimensions and vertex fields, are rejected with logarithmic workspace in their actual length. A validity check does not need to store the matrix. The representation is an explicit string, not an adjacency oracle or a circuit describing a much larger graph.

The computation uses a fixed finite program, a read-only input tape bounded by endmarkers, and a fixed number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. Heads move by ordinary Turing-machine steps. Space is the total number of distinct work-tape cells visited during the computation, including blank cells crossed by heads, all counters, stacks and auxiliary records. The finite control and read-only input cells are uncharged. There is no advice depending on input size, oracle, random tape, external storage, writable input or extra tape whose contents can temporarily be borrowed. The output is a single accept/reject decision. Input rescanning and arbitrary finite computation are permitted, but every input must eventually halt.

The class \(\mathrm{L}\) consists of languages of binary strings decided by such deterministic machines using \(O(\log(N+2))\) space. The class \(\mathrm{NL}\) uses a fixed finite nondeterministic transition relation with the same space bound: an input is accepted exactly when at least one computation branch accepts. One may require a polynomial clock on every branch without changing NL. A logarithmic-space configuration has only polynomially many possibilities, including input-head positions; any accepting computation can therefore be shortened and a logarithmic-size clock suffices. A halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine automatically runs in polynomial time because a repeated complete configuration would repeat forever.

Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions. Such a reduction writes one polynomial-length instance and preserves its yes/no answer while using logarithmic workspace; output bits can be recomputed when composing it with another small-space machine. Thus a positive answer for the specified matrix representation implies \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{L}\), and \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\) already holds.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\), using the stated uniform machine model. An affirmative reachability solution must specify one machine and a constant, and prove correctness, termination, malformed-input handling and the space bound on every input. A negative solution must exclude every such machine: equivalently, for every always-halting correct deterministic reachability decider and every constant \(C\), some valid instance exceeds \(C\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) visited work cells. A class-based argument must establish the equivalence to this concrete reachability target. A lower bound for one search procedure, or a successful algorithm restricted to undirected graphs, using advice, nondeterminism or a higher power of logarithmic space, is insufficient. No numerical approximation of a resource bound answers this exact class-equality question.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in \(O(s^{2})\) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\), so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams give two fixed algorithms with a per-graph guarantee: at least one succeeds, either solving directed reachability in deterministic polynomial time and polylogarithmic space, or estimating length-n random-walk probabilities in nondeterministic logarithmic space. Both report failure and always respect their resource bounds. This alternative does not provide a deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm on all graphs.

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary graph search can remember which vertices have been visited. Logarithmic space holds only a constant number of vertex names and counters, so a separate visited bit for each vertex does not fit. Repeated scans of the input are free of a space penalty, but any saved information between scans counts.

Directed reachability captures an entire complexity class because a small-space machine has only polynomially many configurations. Its legal next steps form the edges of a directed graph, and acceptance is reachability of an accepting configuration. This correspondence is computable with logarithmic workspace.

Savitch’s theorem gives deterministic reachability using \(O((\log n)^2)\) workspace, with a quasipolynomial time bound. The gap between one and two logarithmic factors is exactly relevant to membership in L: an always-halting deterministic machine using only logarithmic space has polynomially many configurations, and hence polynomial running time.

Reingold’s theorem meets the logarithmic-space target when edges are undirected. Directed graphs therefore cannot be replaced by their undirected versions: forgetting an arrow can create paths absent from the original instance.

The equality \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) means that nondeterministic logarithmic space can recognize both reachability and nonreachability. It is a closure theorem within the nondeterministic model, and does not establish that either task has a deterministic logarithmic-space algorithm.

The 2025 alternative links graph connectivity to random-walk estimation, but its successful procedure may differ from graph to graph. Its deterministic branch uses polylogarithmic rather than logarithmic space. Neither qualification disappears merely because both algorithms signal their own failures.

The 2026 hardness result locates the difficulty even in graphs whose edges split into two sets, each a collection of directed paths of length at most two. This remains NL-hard when the decomposition is part of the input. The pieces are simple, but paths using edges from both pieces can still express general directed reachability.

cards.title: Minimum Circuit Size Problem
cards.formal:
Is the Minimum Circuit Size Problem (MCSP), with a complete truth table as input, NP-complete under uniform deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Equivalently, does there exist one deterministic polynomial-time function \(g\) such that
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad x\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ g(x)\in\mathrm{MCSP}?\]
Use the exact circuit model and language below. The target is unconditional and unrelativized. A reduction may not use random bits, advice, an oracle, a gap promise, a partial truth table or an implicitly represented truth table.

source_formulation.text: The primary source asks whether ordinary MCSP is NP-hard and separately whether it may be in BPP. The two previously consolidated sources also explicitly ask about NP-hardness. This card takes their common NP-hardness question as its single target and fixes deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions.

context_blocks.text: MCSP asks whether a fully specified Boolean function has a short circuit. Finding a short representation is an optimization task; this decision version asks whether a proposed size threshold can be met. Its input already contains every function value, which makes checking a proposed circuit efficient.

The main target is the NP-hardness question shared by the three source passages consolidated into this card with user approval on 12 September 2026. The original primary passage also raises membership in BPP. That broader classification is retained here as context rather than being silently identified with the negation of NP-hardness.

The circuit basis matters for exact minimization. The 2026 source treats both counting all gates and counting only binary gates; this card explicitly uses its total-gate convention. The source continues to identify ordinary MCSP hardness as open and distinguishes it from successful hardness results for partial specifications.

Austrin and Risse establish strong lower bounds for sum-of-squares refutations of formulas asserting that a small circuit exists. Sum-of-squares is a particular algebraic proof system. Its limitations give information about a restricted method of certifying circuit lower bounds, without proving that every efficient algorithm for ordinary MCSP fails.

Hirahara and Ilango obtain deterministic quasipolynomial-time nonadaptive hardness, including constant-factor approximation, under three assumptions together: subexponentially secure noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs for SAT, almost-everywhere subexponential nondeterministic circuit lower bounds for coNP, and almost-everywhere near-maximum circuit lower bounds for \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{NP}}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here nonadaptive means that a reduction prepares all oracle questions before receiving answers. Both its assumptions and its longer running time distinguish this result from the target.

The June 2026 ECCC manuscript studies an implicit version whose function is represented by a circuit sampling labeled examples, rather than by the full table. Its randomized gap-hardness result assumes subexponential versions of indistinguishability obfuscation and the nonexistence of an optimal propositional proof system. This is further progress on a related representation, not an unconditional many-one reduction to the language defined here.

cards.definitions:
For \(n\ge1\), an \(n\)-input Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with inputs \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), optional constant sources 0 and 1, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and one designated output wire. Wires may feed arbitrarily many gates. An input, a constant or a gate may be the output. The size is the total number of AND, OR and NOT gates; input and constant sources, wires and the output designation are not charged. In particular, NOT gates count. Write \(\operatorname{CC}(f)\) for the minimum such size computing \(f\) on every input. This fixes the total-gate convention, corresponding to the source's \(R\) size measure. It is not the measure that counts only binary gates, nor the basis of all two-input Boolean functions.

The truth table \(t\in\{0,1\}^{N}\), where \(N=2^n\), lists the values of a total function \(f_t:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) in lexicographic input order. A well-formed instance is \((t,s)\), with integer \(0\le s\le N\) written in binary. It is a yes-instance exactly when \(\operatorname{CC}(f_t)\le s\). To fix a binary language, encode a pair as \(1^{|t|}0t\operatorname{bin}(s)\), with no leading zeros in \(\operatorname{bin}(s)\), except that zero is encoded as the single bit 0. Strings failing this syntax, the power-of-two length requirement, \(n\ge1\), or the threshold bound are no-instances. The input length is \(2N+1+O(\log(N+1))\), so polynomial time is measured in the full truth-table length, not merely in the number \(n\) of variables. The redundant unary length prefix is only a fixed efficiently decodable pair encoding.

Constants have been made explicit to remove a convention left implicit in the source. For a nonconstant function, constant inputs can be eliminated gate by gate without increasing size, so allowing them does not change its optimum. For the two constant functions the answer follows directly from the specified convention. No claim that all Boolean bases preserve exact optimum sizes is needed.

A deterministic polynomial-time function is computed by one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts on every input of length \(m\) within \(C(m+1)^d\) steps, for some constants \(C,d\). It has no advice or oracle. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(L\) to \(K\) is such a function \(g\) satisfying \(x\in L\) if and only if \(g(x)\in K\) for every binary string \(x\). Its output is one ordinary instance, whose entire description is written within that time bound. SAT is satisfiability of finite Boolean formulas over AND, OR and NOT in a fixed explicit binary syntax; malformed formulas are no-instances. Any two usual efficiently interconvertible formula encodings give the same reduction question.

NP consists of languages for which a yes-instance has a certificate of polynomial length that a uniform deterministic polynomial-time machine verifies, with no certificate accepted on a no-instance. A language is NP-hard here if every language in NP reduces to it by the specified many-one reductions, and NP-complete if it is also in NP. MCSP is in NP: a circuit with at most \(s\le N\) gates has an explicit topologically ordered description of \(O(N\log(N+1))\) bits, and evaluating it on all \(N\) assignments checks the entire table in polynomial time. Thus the displayed SAT reduction suffices, by SAT's NP-completeness, and its nonexistence would refute NP-completeness under this reduction convention.

For context only, P denotes uniform deterministic polynomial time and BPP uniform randomized polynomial time with worst-case polynomial running time and error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The source also asks whether MCSP might lie in BPP. That is a separate proposition, not the logical negation of NP-hardness: the two possibilities are not an unconditional exhaustive or disjoint classification.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the displayed SAT-to-MCSP reduction. A positive answer must specify a uniform deterministic reduction, prove its polynomial running time and output length, and prove the yes/no equivalence for every input using the exact total truth-table and gate-count conventions above. A negative answer must prove that every deterministic polynomial-time candidate reduction fails on some input. A conditional theorem, an oracle-relative theorem, hardness under randomized or quasipolynomial-time reductions, a lower bound for a restricted proof system, or hardness of a partial, implicit or gap variant does not alone meet this criterion. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this exact language-reduction statement.

Hirahara and Ilango obtain deterministic quasipolynomial-time nonadaptive hardness, including constant-factor approximation, under three assumptions together: subexponentially secure noninteractive witness-indistinguishable proofs for SAT, almost-everywhere subexponential nondeterministic circuit lower bounds for coNP, and almost-everywhere near-maximum circuit lower bounds for \(\mathrm{P}^{\mathrm{NP}}/\mathrm{poly}\). Here nonadaptive means that a reduction prepares all oracle questions before receiving answers. Both its assumptions and its longer running time distinguish this result from the target.

The June 2026 ECCC manuscript studies an implicit version whose function is represented by a circuit sampling labeled examples, rather than by the full table. Its randomized gap-hardness result assumes subexponential versions of indistinguishability obfuscation and the nonexistence of an optimal propositional proof system. This is further progress on a related representation, not an unconditional many-one reduction to the language defined here.

benchmark_focus.reason: MCSP asks how hard it is to recognize computational simplicity from complete data. Its classification connects NP-completeness with circuit lower bounds, learning and cryptography. A proof or refutation of standard NP-hardness would settle a central question about whether circuit minimization has the same reduction-based difficulty as general NP search.

cards.title: P versus PSPACE
cards.formal: Does every language decidable by a deterministic Turing machine using polynomial working space have a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a machine A and constants C,k such that A decides truth of every closed quantified Boolean formula of encoded length n in at most $C(n+1)^k$ steps?
cards.definitions: P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed polynomial worst-case time bound. PSPACE consists of languages decided by one deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input and visits at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) work-tape cells, for some constants C,k, on inputs of length n. The input is read-only and is not charged as work space; a fixed finite tape alphabet is used. PSPACE imposes no polynomial time bound. A closed quantified Boolean formula has the form \(Q_{1}x_{1}\cdots Q_{m}x_{m} \varphi (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m})\), where each \(Q_{i}\) is \(\exists\) or \(\forall\), quantified variables are distinct, and \(\varphi\) is an explicitly encoded Boolean formula using AND, OR, and NOT, with no free variables. Every quantifier ranges over \(\{0,1\}\). The number of quantifiers and their alternations may grow with n; the input is not restricted to a fixed number of blocks. Use any standard explicit binary encoding, reject malformed inputs, and count its full bit length n. Truth means the usual nested Boolean quantifier semantics. This language, TQBF, is PSPACE-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions. No oracle, advice, randomization, or promise is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) or \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\). The first outcome asserts a deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure for every polynomial-space language; the second asserts a polynomial-space language with no deterministic polynomial-time decision procedure.
cards.why: This asks whether reusing a feasible amount of memory can provide computational power beyond feasible running time. It is a central unresolved separation even when the allowed language class is enlarged from NP to all of PSPACE, and it organizes the complexity of quantified reasoning, games, and verification.

context_blocks.text: Time measures the total number of computation steps; space measures how much information the machine retains at once. Space can be reused. For example, a machine can evaluate a quantified formula by recursively exploring possible choices and reusing its work area when it returns from a branch. The resulting computation may inspect exponentially many choices while keeping only a polynomial amount of information.

Alternating quantifiers express a finite game of choices: existential moves try to make the final formula true, and universal moves challenge them. For example, \(\forall x\exists y (y=x)\) is true because y may depend on x, whereas \(\exists y\forall x (y=x)\) is false. Both variables range over \(\{0,1\}\). A winning strategy for a longer formula can have exponentially many branches even though each play has polynomial length. Polynomial-time alternation captures exactly PSPACE.

The inclusion \(\mathrm{P}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\) is immediate, but its strictness is unknown. \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) would imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{PSPACE}\) because \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}\). A proof of \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), however, would collapse the polynomial hierarchy without automatically giving a polynomial-time algorithm for formulas with an unbounded number of quantifier alternations. This separates the present question from merely solving satisfiability.

The theorem \(\mathrm{IP}=\mathrm{PSPACE}\) characterizes the same space class through interaction: a polynomial-time randomized verifier can check claims from an unbounded prover using a bounded-error interactive protocol. The prover’s assistance is a resource. Removing the prover to obtain an ordinary deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is not a consequence of that characterization.

Williams’ time-to-space simulation gives a concrete advance in the comparison of these resources. For time bounds \(t(n)\ge n, a\) time-t multitape computation can be simulated in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) working space. A consequence is that some linear-space languages require time \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) for every \(\varepsilon >0\). The lower-bound exponent remains bounded: the result does not exhibit a polynomial-space language outside every polynomial time bound.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a single uniform, always-correct Las Vegas program whose expected running time is at most Cn on every admissible (n,w,input), for one C independent of n and w. A negative answer must show that every such sorting program has unbounded expected-time/n ratio over these inputs. A lower bound only for comparison sorting, deterministic programs, or a different word instruction set does not establish that negation.
cards.why: A basic limit on what word-level arithmetic can accomplish beyond comparisons. The challenge is a uniform bound across all word lengths, rather than the already solved polynomial-universe or sufficiently-large-word cases.

Searches through 11 September 2026 found no result settling this full target. Recent parallel sorting results for keys in \([n]\) concern a restricted universe and a different performance model.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

For bounded-integer inputs on a word RAM, a linear-time algorithm for sorting arbitrary word-sized integers would also sort the explicitly generated pairwise sums in quadratic time, allowing a constant-factor increase in word length for the sums. The present target instead allows arbitrary exact real inputs, without floor or bit extraction. An integer-sorting result therefore does not automatically answer this real-RAM question.

cards.title: Size-bounded approximate multicommodity-flow sparsifiers
cards.formal: Does there exist a function \(f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\times(0,1)\to\mathbb N\) such that every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G\) with a labelled set \(T\) of \(k\) terminals admits a finite undirected capacitated graph \(H\), containing the same labelled terminals and at most \(f(k,\varepsilon)\) vertices, for which \[\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\le\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\le(1+\varepsilon)\operatorname{cong}_H(d)\] holds simultaneously for every nonnegative terminal demand vector \(d\)? Here \(0<\varepsilon<1\), and new nonterminal vertices and arbitrary capacities in \(H\) are permitted.
cards.definitions:
A capacitated graph has finitely many vertices, undirected edges and strictly positive finite real capacities \(c_e\). Zero-capacity edges may be deleted and parallel edges combined by summing capacities. The terminals are distinct designated vertices. A demand vector assigns a nonnegative real number \(d_{st}\) to each unordered pair of distinct terminals \(\{s,t\}\).

For each terminal pair, assign nonnegative flow amounts to the finitely many simple paths joining the pair, so that their sum is \(d_{st}\). Commodities may split across paths. The load on an edge is the sum of the assigned amounts over all paths using it, regardless of direction or commodity. The congestion of a routing is \(\max_e \operatorname{load}(e)/c_e\). Define \(\operatorname{cong}_G(d)\) as the infimum over all such routings; set it to infinity if some positive demand cannot be routed. Zero demand has congestion zero, including in an edgeless graph. Inequalities involving infinity use the extended nonnegative reals. Integral, unsplittable and directed flow models are not intended.

Equivalently, let \(P_G\) be the set of demand vectors routable with loads at most the capacities. The requirement is \(P_G\subseteq P_H\subseteq(1+\varepsilon)P_G\), where scalar multiplication multiplies every demand coordinate. This fixes the one-sided normalization of quality. A single \(H\) must work for all demands; choosing a different graph after seeing \(d\) is not allowed.

Size means the number of vertices, including terminals. For simple graphs it also bounds the number of edges quadratically, but no bound on the bit complexity of real capacities is required. The bound is uniform over original graph size, topology and capacity magnitudes. This is an existence question: no efficient construction algorithm or computability requirement on \(f\) is added. The graph \(H\) may be entirely new and need not be a minor, quotient, contraction or subgraph of \(G\). Exact preservation corresponds to zero error and is outside the stated positive-error domain.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence statement, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A negative answer must provide fixed \(k\) and fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) for which no finite vertex bound works for all input graphs. Exact-sparsifier lower bounds alone, or lower bounds restricted to contraction-based sparsifiers, do not refute this statement. A positive answer must produce a graph realizing the simultaneous routing inequalities; a non-graph encoding of feasible demands does not suffice.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.

The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

benchmark_focus.reason: Tests whether preserving all cuts of a multiway interaction system requires any more hyperedges than the graph sparsification upper bound. It separates the number of retained interactions from their incidence storage and from the cost of computing them.

cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal:
Is there a uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm that lists all attainable subset sums up to a given threshold in time near-linear in the explicit input size plus the number of distinct output values?

More precisely, for integers \(n,t\ge1\) and an input list \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\), put
\[
S(X,t)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}x_i:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\right\}
\cap\{0,\ldots,t\},\qquad q(X,t)=|S(X,t)|.
\]
Does there exist one finite program \(A\), a fixed integer \(d\ge1\), a constant \(C>0\), and an integer \(b\ge0\), chosen independently of every input, such that on the word RAM defined below, with
\[
w=d\left\lceil\log_2(n+t+2)\right\rceil,
\]
both of the following hold for every valid \(n,t,X\)?
\[
\forall r\quad T_{A,d}(X,t;r)
\le C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b,
\]
\[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]\ge \frac23.
\]
Here success means that the complete output lists every element of \(S(X,t)\) exactly once and no other value. The time bound applies to every random execution, including unsuccessful executions. The algorithm is not given \(q(X,t)\) or any subset-sum information as additional input.

This card retains the previously selected bounded-error, worst-case word-RAM formulation of the source's near-linear output-sensitive question. Its explicit instruction set and requirement on every random execution are editorial model conventions; the source's expected-time or high-probability bounds are reported separately below.
cards.definitions:
The input is a list of \(n\) positive integers and an integer threshold \(t\), with \(1\le x_i\le t\). Repeated values represent distinct available items, and each index may be selected at most once. Thus the input is an explicitly listed multiset, not a binary encoding of item multiplicities. The empty subset contributes zero. The set \(S(X,t)\) contains distinct integer sums, not a count of subsets. The required output is a finite sequence of \(q(X,t)\) integers in arbitrary order, containing each element of \(S(X,t)\) once. There is no requirement to output witnessing subsets. The threshold is inclusive.

For each fixed choice of \(d\), a word holds an unsigned integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The input occupies a read-only word array containing \(n,t,x_1,\ldots,x_n\) at addresses \(0,1,\ldots,n+1\), one integer per cell; these values fit in a word. Reading that array at a larger address returns zero. The machine starts at its designated first instruction, with register zero containing \(w\) and all other registers zero. Its separate writable memory consists of word-addressed cells with addresses in the same range, initially zero. Initially zero memory is a machine convention, not an instruction that scans the entire address space. Every initialization performed by the program, and every subsequent memory access, is charged. A computation has a fixed finite control and a fixed finite number of word registers; additional storage uses the charged memory instructions.

Each of the following is a unit-cost instruction on a fixed number of words: copying; reading one addressed input word; loading or storing one addressed writable word; comparing unsigned words and conditional branching; bitwise Boolean operations; logical left or right shifts; addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\); integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; generating one independent uniform random word; and appending one word to the output. A shift by an amount at least \(w\) returns zero. Arithmetic on larger integers must be implemented using these instructions and is charged accordingly. The program may use fixed integer constants encoded in its finite description, interpreted modulo \(2^w\) when placed in a word. It has no advice, input-dependent tables, or additional oracle instructions. Tables constructed during a run are allowed and all their construction costs count. A halt instruction ends the output sequence and costs one step; an invalid operation, such as division by zero, halts with failure. Output words already appended cannot be withdrawn.

One finite program and one constant \(d\) must serve all \(n,t,X\); neither the program nor its constants may vary with the input parameters. This is the uniformity requirement. All input reads, preprocessing, random-word generation, internal computation and output writes count toward running time. The memory bound comes only from word addressing; no further space restriction is imposed.

For a fixed input and \(d\), let \(r=(r_1,r_2,\ldots)\) be an infinite sequence of independent uniform words from \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), consumed in order by random-word instructions. This product distribution defines \(\Pr_r\). A deterministic program is permitted as a special case that ignores \(r\). Let \(T_{A,d}(X,t;r)\) be the number of executed instructions, or \(+\infty\) for a nonhalting run. The event \(\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\) means that the run halts normally and its output sequence has exactly the required distinct values. Failure includes a missing sum, an extra value, a duplicate, an invalid operation or nontermination. The probability guarantee concerns this single event for the entire output, rather than a separate probability for each attainable value. The condition on time includes even random sequences having probability zero as individual infinite sequences.

The logarithm is base two, and \(b\) is any fixed nonnegative integer. Allowing an arbitrary fixed real exponent \(b\ge0\) would give the same existence question, since rounding that exponent up only enlarges this bound. The notation \(\widetilde O\) used in the context suppresses fixed powers of logarithms in the specified parameters; the displayed bound itself is the exact target. In particular, dependence polynomial in the numerical threshold \(t\), or in \(q(X,t)\) beyond its first power, is not hidden in the target's logarithmic factor.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum can have a sparse set of attainable values below a very large threshold. The output-sensitive target measures the work against that set and the explicit input, while still requiring exact enumeration.

Bringmann and Nakos explicitly ask for a \(\widetilde O(|S(X,t)|)\)-time algorithm. Their inspected revision gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(|S(X,t)|^{4/3})\) bound with high probability; its formal subset-sum definition includes the threshold itself. This card includes the input-reading term needed for an explicit multiset.

Bringmann, Fischer and Nakos give a randomized \(\widetilde O(|S(X,t)|\sqrt n)\)-time algorithm and explicitly leave the near-linear output-sensitive endpoint open. Their probability guarantees and multiset conventions are stated separately, rather than implying a bound for every random execution.

Chan proves deterministic output-sensitive bounds \(\widetilde O(|S(X,t)|^{4/3})\) and \(\widetilde O(|S(X,t)|\sqrt n)\), as well as deterministic pseudopolynomial time \(\widetilde O(t)\). The inspected paper allows polylogarithmic factors in \(n,t\) and separately discusses the input-reading cost for explicit multisets. These bounds do not attain the endpoint on this card.

The card preserves its existing bounded-error word-RAM target with time bounded on every random execution. This fixes the previously chosen model precisely; it does not identify expected-time, high-probability-time and worst-case-time guarantees as interchangeable.

cards.why: The question tests whether a basic dynamic-programming problem can be solved at essentially the cost of reading its input and writing its distinct answers. A positive resolution would avoid paying for a large unused numerical range even when the input contains repeated items. A negative resolution would establish an additional computational cost beyond input and output size for a fundamental exact problem. This is a general algorithmic endpoint, not a request to count solutions or to improve one implementation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the formal existence assertion or its full logical negation, using exactly the input, machine, randomness, output and cost conventions above.

A positive answer must specify one finite program \(A\) and constants \(d\ge1\), \(C>0\), and \(b\ge0\), with \(d,b\) integers, and prove for every valid input both the running-time bound on every random execution and probability at least \(2/3\) of the complete correct output. The constants may depend on the program but not on \(n,t,X\). An expected-time estimate or a bound that holds only with high probability does not by itself prove the required bound on every execution.

A negative answer must prove the following full negation. For every finite program \(A\) in the defined model, every integer \(d\ge1\), every constant \(C>0\), and every integer \(b\ge0\), there exist integers \(n,t\ge1\) and a list \(X\in\{1,\ldots,t\}^{n}\) such that
\[
\left[
\exists r\quad
T_{A,d}(X,t;r)>
C\bigl(n+q(X,t)\bigr)\bigl(\log_2(n+t+2)\bigr)^b
\right]
\quad\lor\quad
\left[
\Pr_r\!\left[\operatorname{Success}_{A,d}(X,t;r)\right]<\frac23
\right].
\]
The defeating input may depend on \(A,d,C,b\), so no single fixed instance must defeat all algorithms. A lower bound only for a restricted class of algorithms does not establish this negation. A conditional lower bound proves only its conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also established. The target is an exact existence question about an asymptotic resource bound; numerical \(1/100\) approximation does not replace either required proof.

cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

context_blocks.text: This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts \(T(n)=(n- 1)^{2}\). Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.

Writable-annotation complementation and bounded-input-length simulations are separate results.

context_blocks.text: All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over \(\{0,1\}\), consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least \(2^{r}\) states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses \(O(r)\) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in \(a_{1}*\cdots a_{t}\)* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ July 2026 revision proves a quadratic state lower bound for deterministic two-way automata solving one-way liveness. The problem encodes paths through successive layers of a graph; a small nondeterministic automaton can guess a path, whereas a deterministic one must use more control states. The lower bound also applies to conversion from one-way NFAs. Quadratic growth is compatible with the polynomial simulation asked here, so this strengthens the documented lower-bound picture without resolving the conjecture.
