cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.

cards.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. cards.context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least \(n^{2}\) possible queries, while the stored representation has only \(O(n \log ^{3} n)\) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is \(O(\log  n)\), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is \(\Omega (\min \{\log (m/s), n/\log  s\})\) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most \(O(\log  n)\). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. This is not an unconditional impossibility theorem for stronger lower bounds. The authors’ errata also flag a new sampling method whose coverage had not been checked and explain why a previously cited rigidity consequence no longer constitutes an unachieved barrier.

Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.title: Deterministic fully dynamic connectivity with polylogarithmic worst-case updates
cards.formal:
Does there exist a finite deterministic word-RAM program \(A\), with fixed positive integer constants \(C,c,d,a\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) it maintains an initially empty simple undirected graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) under every finite valid online sequence of edge insertions, edge deletions and pairwise connectivity queries, with all the following guarantees?
\[\begin{aligned}
 \text{initialization time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{total stored words at every time}&\le Cn^d,\\
 \text{time of each individual operation}&\le C(\log_2 n)^c.
\end{aligned}\]
Every query must return the exact connectivity bit. Initialization receives only \(n\); the word size is \(w=\lceil a\log_2 n\rceil\), and computation uses the machine conventions below. All constants and the same finite program are chosen before \(n\) or the operation sequence. Give a complete Lean proof of this existence proposition or its logical negation.
cards.definitions:
A graph state is a set \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:u,v\in[n],\ u\ne v\}\), initially empty. An operation has a tag and two vertex labels, each supplied as one word. A valid \(\operatorname{insert}(u,v)\) requires distinct endpoints and an absent edge, and adds that edge. A valid \(\operatorname{delete}(u,v)\) requires a present edge and removes it. A query \(\operatorname{connected}(u,v)\) is valid for any \(u,v\in[n]\) and outputs one bit. Its answer is one exactly when there is a finite sequence \(u=x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_k=v\), with \(k\ge0\), whose consecutive pairs are edges of the current graph. In particular, a vertex is connected to itself. The graph has no additional promise on density, planarity, degree or expansion.

The machine must finish the current operation before the next is supplied. No operation count, future sequence, or complete input graph is available during initialization. The guarantee applies to every finite valid sequence of arbitrary length, including sequences selected using all previously observable states and answers. Persistent memory is bounded in terms of \(n\) alone, independently of the elapsed number of operations. Past output is write-only and cannot serve as free external storage.

Fix a word RAM with a finite instruction list and a fixed finite number of word registers. Words are unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\); memory addresses are also words. Each indirect load or store, register copy, comparison, conditional branch, Boolean bitwise operation, shift, and arithmetic operation on at most two words costs one step. Arithmetic primitives are addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient and remainder. Addition, subtraction and multiplication return their result modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder use unsigned integer division and a zero divisor causes failure. A left shift discards bits outside the word; a right shift fills with zeros; either returns zero when the shift amount is at least \(w\). Reading an input word and writing the query bit also cost one step. The finite program can contain fixed integer constants, interpreted modulo \(2^w\), but has no oracle, random instruction, advice string or input-size-dependent instruction table. Any longer arithmetic computation pays for all constituent instructions.

Mutable registers and allocated memory, including every table and representation of the graph, count toward the stated space bound. Initially they contain only zeros except for the input \(n\); data-dependent initialization, allocation and zeroing of allocated words are charged. Every addressed location must be allocated and have a representable address. The fixed coefficient \(a\) may be chosen sufficiently large for the program's polynomial space; it cannot depend on \(n\) or sequence length. Polynomial preprocessing may depend only on \(n\), and all its computation and stored output count toward the initialization and space bounds. The program and its fixed finite control are independent of \(n\).

Time includes all graph maintenance, rebuilding, memory management, query computation and response output performed during that operation. No background work between operations is free. The operation bound is a worst-case bound for each individual call, not an average over a sequence or an expectation. Using positive integer constants is a normalization of the original polynomial-space and polylogarithmic-time bounds: enlarging constants or exponents absorbs fixed factors and small input sizes. It imposes no graph restriction.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of either
\[\exists A\ \exists C,c,d,a\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge2\ \forall s\in\mathcal S_n,\quad \operatorname{Guarantees}(A,C,c,d,a,n,s),\]
or its logical negation. Here \(A\) ranges over the finite deterministic programs just defined, \(\mathcal S_n\) is the set of all finite valid operation sequences, and \(\operatorname{Guarantees}\) includes initialization, termination, exact answers, memory use and the per-operation bounds in the statement. A positive answer must establish all guarantees for one program and constants that work for every \(n,s\). A negative answer must rule out every such program and every constant choice, equivalently show that each candidate fails a required guarantee for some size and finite valid sequence, with the empty sequence also testing initialization. Failure to terminate is a failure of the applicable time bound.

All memory and running-time statements must refer to the specified machine semantics. A lower bound for a restricted family of implementations, a single counterexample to one proposed algorithm, or a theorem requiring an unproved complexity assumption does not negate the full proposition. An amortized, randomized, expected-time, restricted-graph or offline guarantee does not prove it. This is an existence question, with no numerical tolerance or weaker intermediate target.
cards.why: Exact dynamic connectivity is a basic test of whether a graph data structure can guarantee uniformly low latency without randomness. The question separates efficient processing of a long sequence from a fast response after every individual change, and is relevant to graph algorithms that call connectivity as a subroutine.

context_blocks.text: Connectivity asks whether two vertices lie in the same component, not for a shortest path or an explicit list of all vertices in that component. Deleting an edge can change this answer for many pairs simultaneously. The required output is still only the queried bit; the target concerns how much work must be charged to each operation.

Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic structure with \(O(\log^2 n)\) amortized update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) connectivity query time. Their guarantee controls the total work over a sequence, while permitting an expensive individual update. It does not establish the per-operation guarantee asked here.

Kapron, King and Mountjoy give worst-case bounds \(O(\log^4 n)\) for insertion, \(O(\log^5 n)\) for deletion and \(O(\log n/\log\log n)\) for queries. Their randomized structure has one-sided error: a reported connection is valid, but a reported disconnection can be wrong with small probability. This does not give the exact deterministic guarantee.

Chuzhoy and coauthors establish deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case update time. This notation permits functions growing more quickly than every fixed power of \(\log n\), for example \(\exp(\sqrt{\log n})\). Consequently a subpolynomial bound alone leaves a gap to the fixed polylogarithm in this card.

Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg’s SODA 2026 Theorem 1.1 is Las Vegas: it maintains a correct spanning forest with polylogarithmic expected worst-case update time. Its guarantee even allows an adaptive adversary observing the internal state and random bits. The expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness for an operation, rather than amortization over operations; it remains different from a deterministic bound on every execution. Theorem 1.3 gives a conditional deterministic result, not an unconditional resolution of this card.

Pătraşcu and Demaine prove \(\max\{t_u,t_q\}=\Omega(\log n)\), together with update–query tradeoffs, in the cell-probe model with \(O(\log n)\)-bit cells. Here \(t_u\) and \(t_q\) measure update and query cost. The bound applies even to disjoint paths and permits amortization and randomization. Cell probes count memory accesses while allowing free computation, so a bound there also constrains a word RAM. A logarithmic lower bound is compatible with the requested polylogarithmic upper bound.

As checked on 15 September 2026, the official FOCS 2026 accepted-paper list includes Dynamic Connectivity, Minimum Spanning Tree, and 2-Edge Connectivity with Polylogarithmic Worst-Case Update Time, by Simon Meierhans, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg and Yu-Cheng Yeh. The inspected entry provides a title and authors, with no theorem or manuscript link. It does not specify whether the guarantee is deterministic. The current status is therefore recorded as uncertain; this announcement is neither treated as a verified matching solution nor ignored in favor of an older open-problem statement.

Probst Gutenberg’s publication page independently lists the same FOCS 2026 title and coauthors, again without a manuscript link in that entry. The conference is scheduled for November 2026; its acceptance announcement is distinct from an inspected proceedings paper. A complete statement is needed to decide whether the result meets this exact deterministic target.

cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal:
For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized fully dynamic algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon,a}\) and constants \(K,d,B\ge1\) with the following guarantees?

For every \(n\ge2\) and every valid oblivious sequence of \(T\le n^a\) edge insertions and deletions starting from the empty graph on \([n]\), the expected total initialization and update cost is at most
\[
K\left[n+T\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\right].
\]
With probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\), after every update the algorithm maintains an explicit matching \(M\) in the current graph \(G\) such that
\[
|M|\ge\frac{\nu(G)}{1+\varepsilon},
\]
where \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality. The same constants apply to every \(n,T\) and sequence for the fixed \(\varepsilon,a\).
cards.definitions:
At all times the graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, with the fixed vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Initially there are no edges. One update inserts an absent edge or deletes a present edge; only valid update sequences are required to be handled. The graph need not be bipartite or have bounded degree.

A matching is a subset of the current edges in which no vertex belongs to more than one edge. The integer \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum possible number of edges in a matching, and it is zero for an edgeless graph. The algorithm stores a mate array \(\operatorname{mate}[1..n]\): zero means unmatched, while a nonzero value \(\operatorname{mate}[v]=u\) must have \(u\ne v\), \(\operatorname{mate}[u]=v\) and \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Together with its stored cardinality, this explicitly represents \(M\). A size estimate or a fractional assignment to edges is not this representation.

After each completed update, reading the mate of any specified vertex or reading \(|M|\) takes at most a fixed constant number of word operations. Listing the full matching may scan the array in \(O(n)\) time, and need not be performed after every update. All work needed to modify the representation, including every changed array entry and the cardinality, counts toward update cost. External requests to read or list the maintained matching are charged their stated query costs separately; they do not excuse extra update work.

The update sequence is oblivious: for each guarantee it is any fixed sequence independent of the algorithm’s random bits. Updates are delivered one at a time, and the algorithm must finish processing one before seeing the next. It knows \(n\) and has the fixed parameters \(\varepsilon,a\), but the future sequence and its actual length are not supplied in advance. This is distinct from a computation receiving all updates at once, and it makes no guarantee against an adversary choosing updates from observed random-dependent outputs.

Use a word-RAM with word length \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with \(B\) a fixed positive integer for the algorithm. Memory cells have word addresses and initially contain zero; every access or write costs an operation, and untouched cells require no initialization work. The instruction set consists of word reads and writes, indirect addressing, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. A fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one operation. Stored random words and intermediate values use ordinary memory. Larger integers must use multiple words, with all operations charged; no arbitrary-precision operation, graph oracle or precomputed instance advice is available. No additional linear-space restriction is imposed.

Expectation is over the algorithm’s private randomness on each fixed sequence and includes the entire initialization and all \(T\) updates. The bound is amortized over that sequence, not a worst-case bound on each individual update. The required finite expectation includes termination with probability one. Separately, one event of probability at least \(1-n^{-3}\) must ensure the valid mate representation and approximation inequality after every update in the sequence simultaneously. A separate probability bound at each time without this joint guarantee is insufficient.

The parameters \(\varepsilon\) and \(a\) are fixed independently of \(n\). The machine and constants may depend on both; no polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) and no uniform compiler taking \(\varepsilon,a\) as inputs is required. Integer \(a\) covers every polynomial sequence-length regime. There is no demand for an infinite update sequence with one global success event. This is an exact existence proposition for the stated approximation scheme and resources, not a numerical question about \(\nu(G)\).
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply algorithms and a complete Lean-checked proof covering every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\), every fixed polynomial horizon, every \(n\), and every valid oblivious sequence, including the expected total cost, representation-access costs and simultaneous success event. Alternatively, give a complete Lean-checked refutation of these quantified guarantees; failure for one fixed accuracy and one fixed horizon exponent, for every admissible algorithm and constants, suffices.

An estimator without explicit matching edges, a fixed approximation factor bounded away from one, a partially dynamic algorithm, an algorithm receiving future updates, or an update bound larger than every fixed power of \(\log n\) does not prove the proposition. A lower bound requiring accuracy to shrink with \(n\), polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), or an adaptive adversary does not by itself refute this weaker stated target. Conditional lower bounds require their hypotheses and are not unconditional negative answers.

cards.title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), determine the worst-case sample-complexity function \(N_\delta(n)\) up to multiplicative constant factors as \(n\to\infty\). This is the least number of independent deletion traces from which one estimator can reconstruct every unknown \(n\)-bit string exactly with probability at least \(2/3\). Computation is unrestricted, the original length and deletion probability are known, and constants may depend on \(\delta\).
cards.definitions:
Observation space. Fix \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\ge2\), and a real \(\delta\in(0,1)\). An arbitrary fixed string \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\) is unknown. A deletion trace independently keeps each input bit with probability \(p=1-\delta\) and concatenates the surviving bits in their original order. The output lies in the finite set
\[\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^k,\]
where \(\{0,1\}^0\) consists of the empty string. The length of each received trace is observable. Its original retained indices and deletion mask are not supplied. There are no substitutions, insertions, reversals, cyclic shifts or alignment labels.

Trace law. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing index tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) with \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). Define \(e_x(\varnothing)=1\). The trace distribution is
\[\mu_{x,\delta}(y)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Different deletion masks producing the same observed string all contribute to this probability. For example, for \(x=00\), the one-bit trace \(0\) has probability \(2(1-\delta)\delta\). All \(m\) observations use independent masks on the same original \(x\), so their joint distribution is \(\mu_{x,\delta}^{\otimes m}\).

Estimators. A randomized estimator for fixed \(n,\delta,m\) is a stochastic kernel \(K\) assigning every observed tuple \(\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m\) a probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\). Thus \(K(\mathbf y,z)\ge0\) and \(\sum_zK(\mathbf y,z)=1\). The kernel may depend on \(n,\delta,m\), but not on the unknown string. It describes all permitted internal randomization; a deterministic estimator assigns probability one to a single output. Its success probability on \(x\) is
\[s_{x,\delta}(K)=\sum_{\mathbf y\in\mathcal Y_n^m}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mu_{x,\delta}(y_j)\right)K(\mathbf y,x).\]
The output must equal the whole original string, with its original linear order. Small edit distance, a list containing the string, or recovery of only some coordinates does not count as success. There is no prior distribution on \(x\); the success inequality must hold separately for every string.

Sample complexity. With \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), set
\[N_\delta(n)=\min\left\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\exists K\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ s_{x,\delta}(K)\ge\frac23\right\}.\]
For \(m=0\), the observation tuple is empty and the product is one. The minimum is finite: a single trace has length \(n\) with probability \((1-\delta)^n>0\), and any such trace equals \(x\). Consequently the probability of receiving at least one complete trace tends to one with the number of independent samples. The cost is the fixed total number of traces, including empty or repeated traces, not their total bit length. Allowing a procedure to use at most \(m\) traces gives the same convention by ignoring unused samples; a bound only on the expected number of observations is not the definition.

Information-theoretic scope. There is no limit on running time, storage, description length or processing between observations, and no computability or uniformity restriction on the kernel family. The real deletion probability is a known mathematical parameter, so no finite encoding or estimation of \(\delta\) is required. These conventions make the question purely statistical. The input string has no codebook, sparsity, separation, random-generation or other promise. The asymptotic limit varies \(n\) while keeping \(\delta\) fixed; a simultaneous guarantee for \(\delta\) depending on \(n\), or uniform constants as \(\delta\) approaches an endpoint, is not required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a positive function \(f_\delta(n)\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), there exist \(0<c_\delta\le C_\delta<\infty\) and an integer \(n_\delta\ge2\) such that
\[c_\delta f_\delta(n)\le N_\delta(n)\le C_\delta f_\delta(n)\qquad(n\ge n_\delta).\]
Finite exceptional lengths may equivalently be absorbed into constants for a positive finite representative \(f_\delta\). Give an informative mathematical description of the growth rate, rather than restating the defining minimum or assigning \(f_\delta=N_\delta\) without determining it.

The upper bound must establish estimators with the stated sample budget and success probability for every string. The lower bound must cover all randomized kernels allowed above, not only a named algorithm, local statistics, efficient computation or a restricted family of observations. Worst-case hard strings may depend on the estimator and sample budget; no single string must defeat every estimator.

The requested constant factors multiply the number of traces itself. Matching only the order of \(\log N_\delta(n)\), a polynomial exponent with an unspecified growing factor, or a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification is insufficient unless it yields the displayed bounds. This asymptotic criterion has no additive \(1/100\) tolerance. Average-case strings, approximate recovery, circular traces, a chosen codebook, or one special deletion probability do not determine the full target.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected July 2026 preprint gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for every fixed retention probability, while the unrestricted lower bound cited by it and the September graph-trace preprint remains polynomial. Neither determines N_delta(n) up to constant factors. Circular, local-SQ, separated-string and graph-trace results have different promises or observation models. No matching resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; source proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: The target asks how the optimal number of observations grows, including its exponent and any unbounded logarithmic factors. Whether some polynomial number of traces suffices is an important unresolved qualitative question within this more precise target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its Theorem 43 bounds the number of traces by \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\) for an absolute constant \(c\), where \(p=1-\delta\). This considerably narrows the earlier gap, but neither proves polynomial sample complexity nor gives matching lower bounds. In particular, it does not determine the multiplicative-constant growth rate requested here.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.context:
The target asks how the optimal number of observations grows, including its exponent and any unbounded logarithmic factors. Whether some polynomial number of traces suffices is an important unresolved qualitative question within this more precise target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

A deletion does not mark its former position. Two different deletion masks can produce the same observed string, even when the original input is fixed. Trace lengths are visible, and an undeleted trace would reveal the entire input, but its probability \((1-\delta)^n\) decays exponentially for a fixed nonzero deletion rate. The definition therefore has a finite elementary upper bound while still leaving room for vastly better sample complexity.

Chase proves a worst-case lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{3/2}/\log^7 n)\) for every fixed deletion probability and constant success threshold. The proof exhibits pairs of strings whose trace laws are hard to distinguish. This is an information-theoretic obstruction, not a running-time hypothesis or a limitation of one reconstruction procedure. It rules out near-linear sample complexity, but is consistent with a larger polynomial bound.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint gives a quasipolynomial sample upper bound for every fixed positive retention probability. Its Theorem 43 bounds the number of traces by \(\exp(p^{-7/3}(\log_2 n)^c)\) for an absolute constant \(c\), where \(p=1-\delta\). This considerably narrows the earlier gap, but neither proves polynomial sample complexity nor gives matching lower bounds. In particular, it does not determine the multiplicative-constant growth rate requested here.

The same paper explicitly separates samples from running time. It gives quasipolynomial sample complexity for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string and quasipolynomial time for distinguishing two supplied candidates. It leaves a quasipolynomial-time general reconstruction algorithm unresolved. Since this card permits unrestricted processing, its upper-bound progress remains relevant even without that further algorithmic guarantee.

A local statistical-query procedure receives approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that restricted model, nearly matching the earlier subexponential sample bound. Their theorem does not apply to arbitrary processing of individual traces. The later general upper bound is therefore compatible with the local-query lower bound.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

A September 2026 preprint studies reconstruction of graph degree sequences from vertex-deleted subgraphs. Its introduction separately cites the quasipolynomial upper bound and polynomial lower bound for binary strings. Its new graph theorems do not supply a matching bound for the linear string observation model of this card.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n\operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal:
Do there exist absolute real constants \(C\geq1\), \(K>0\), \(d\geq0\), an integer word-size constant \(B\geq3\), and one uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A\) such that for every integer \(n\geq1\) and all explicitly given \(x,y\in\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}^n\), every execution uses at most
\[Kn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^d\]
word-RAM instructions and its integer output \(D\) satisfies
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq D\leq C\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\bigr]\geq\frac23?\]
The constants and program are chosen once for all input lengths and all pairs. The distance is unit-cost Levenshtein distance; the probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness on that fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\Sigma_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n^2+1\}\). The input is \(n\geq1\) followed by two arrays of \(n\) symbols from \(\Sigma_n\), stored in consecutive memory cells with one symbol per word. Binary strings and strings over any fixed alphabet are included after relabeling. The arrays are explicitly present; there is no compressed representation, access oracle, preprocessed database or promised input distribution.

The distance \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions that transform \(x\) into \(y\). Inserted and substituted symbols belong to \(\Sigma_n\), and intermediate strings may have any finite length. Each operation has cost one; leaving an equal symbol unchanged has cost zero. No transpositions, block moves, variable symbol weights or affine gap penalties are allowed. A substitution costs one, not two. The optimum is an integer between zero and \(n\).

The word length is \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, with one fixed integer \(B\geq3\) for the algorithm. A word represents an unsigned integer from \(0\) to \(2^w-1\); memory addresses are words and all cells outside the given input are initially zero. The machine has a fixed finite instruction sequence and fixed integer constants, independent of \(n,x,y\). The unit-cost instructions are random-access reads or writes of one word, comparisons, conditional branches, bitwise Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero word divisor. Shifts fill with zeros and discard overflow; a shift amount at least \(w\) gives zero. Address calculations obey the same costs. Larger integers occupy several words and require several charged instructions. No arbitrary-precision arithmetic, advice, oracle or quantum instruction is available.

One fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit random word costs one instruction; its individual bits are independent fair bits, and different draws are independent. All preprocessing, memory operations, random draws and output writing count toward the bound. The output is an integer in signed binary notation. Only its value is requested, not a sequence of edits. Every execution must terminate within the stated bound, including those that produce an incorrect estimate. An incorrect execution may return an integer outside the interval. The success guarantee is separate for every pair, not an average over an input distribution.

The quantifier order is \(\exists C,K,d,B,A\;\forall n,x,y\), followed by the displayed probability and all-execution time requirements. Neither the approximation factor nor the logarithmic exponent may grow with \(n\). There is no promise that the distance is large or positive. In particular, when \(x=y\), successful output must be zero. There is no additive error. The shorthand \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) refers exactly to one bound of the displayed form with fixed \(K,d\), not to \(n^{1+\eta}\) for each fixed \(\eta>0\) or to an arbitrary \(n^{1+o(1)}\) overhead.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of one algorithm and fixed constants meeting both requirements on all input pairs, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must rule out every finite approximation constant, every fixed logarithmic exponent and every permitted randomized algorithm and word-size constant; failure at one chosen factor or for deterministic algorithms alone is insufficient. A conditional lower bound gives only a conditional conclusion unless its hypothesis is also proved. An \(n^{1+\eta}\)-time algorithm for a fixed positive \(\eta\), an approximation factor growing with input length, an additive-error guarantee, an expected-time bound alone, or a theorem only for distant pairs does not settle the question. A large but fixed approximation constant is acceptable. This is an existence question, with no additional numerical approximation tolerance on its answer.
cards.why: This asks whether allowing one universal constant loss of alignment accuracy reduces worst-case sequence comparison to the cost of reading the input, apart from a fixed polylogarithmic overhead. The result would locate a basic computational boundary that remains beyond the known fast constant-factor algorithms. Even a large universal factor would resolve this existence question.

context_blocks.text: Alignment matters because insertions and deletions shift later positions. For \(x=(01)^r\) and \(y=(10)^r\), with \(r\geq1\), every corresponding position differs, while \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)=2\). Thus Hamming distance, which counts unequal corresponding positions, is \(2r\) and is not a universal constant-factor estimate for edit distance. The task concerns the optimum over all alignments.

The multiplicative guarantee includes nearby pairs. Equal strings require successful output zero, and distance-one pairs require an estimate at most the same universal constant used at all lengths. An additive error that grows with length cannot be absorbed into that bound. Reading both complete inputs is allowed; this is a total-runtime question rather than a sublinear-query question.

Andoni and Onak’s early theorem already gives a subpolynomial approximation factor in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, including for binary strings. Here subpolynomial means bounded by \(n^\eta\) eventually for every fixed \(\eta>0\). Such a bound still permits a factor that grows without bound, and an arbitrary subpolynomial runtime overhead need not be a fixed power of a logarithm. Their result therefore does not supply either fixed quantity required on this card.

Koucký and Saks prove a guarantee \(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)\leq U\leq R(\operatorname{ED}(x,y)+n^{1-\zeta})\) with high probability, for constants \(R,\zeta>0\) depending on a fixed runtime parameter. Their full Theorem 1.1 uses time \(\widetilde O(n^{1+1/T})\), with fixed \(T\geq1\); the tilde hides logarithmic factors. This gives a constant factor on sufficiently distant pairs, but the additive term prevents that conclusion uniformly for all distances.

Andoni and Nosatzki remove the distance restriction: for each fixed \(\eta>0\), their algorithm has time \(O(n^{1+\eta})\) and factor \(f(1/\eta)\). Theorem 1.1 of the full manuscript and its following paragraph specify dependence on the runtime slack, described as doubly exponential. Their journal article was published online on August 17, 2026. The publication does not change the fixed-slack theorem into a fixed-polylogarithmic-overhead theorem.

For every fixed \(\eta>0\), the factor \(n^\eta\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of \(\log n\). Making \(\eta\) depend on \(n\) also changes the theorem’s approximation factor and hidden constants. Thus the existing family does not automatically supply one algorithm with fixed \(C,K,d\). The open question is this remaining simultaneous control of approximation and overhead, rather than the already established existence of a strongly subquadratic constant-factor algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 theorem gives a different tradeoff: \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for each fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with stated time \(n^2/2^{\log^{\Omega(1)}n}\). It achieves near-exact accuracy, but its stated runtime does not meet this card’s much smaller overhead. Their separate LCS theorem is not substituted for the ordinary edit-distance theorem.

Backurs and Indyk’s conditional exact-computation result relates a fixed exponent saving for edit distance to a fixed exponential saving for CNF satisfiability. It does not rule out the coarse approximation required here. The known fast constant-factor algorithms already show that approximation must be distinguished from exact computation.

TCS-7220 asks for every fixed \((1+\varepsilon)\) accuracy with some positive fixed saving from exponent two, and TCS-7235 asks for the same accuracy in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time. Neither stated guarantee alone supplies this card’s fixed polylogarithmic overhead. Conversely, one unspecified fixed factor here does not imply arbitrary near-exact accuracy. These user-approved targets remain distinct. Weighted or tree edit distances, codeword promises, quantum algorithms and data structures with separate preprocessing have different models.

cards.title: Existence of complete EFX allocations for additive valuations
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For all integers \(n\ge4\) and \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \((v_{ig})_{i\in[n],g\in[m]}\) of nonnegative real values, does there exist a complete allocation \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) such that \(\sum_{h\in A_i}v_{ih}\ge\sum_{h\in A_j\setminus\{g\}}v_{ih}\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\) and every \(g\in A_j\) satisfying \(v_{ig}>0\)?
cards.why: Asks whether an indivisible allocation can always control every agent’s envy after the removal of any positively valued good, while distributing all goods. It tests a stronger fairness guarantee than EF1 even before imposing computational efficiency.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No resolution of the complete-allocation question for unrestricted nonnegative additive valuations was located. The August 2026 result covers four agents and at most nine goods; nonadditive counterexamples do not meet this model. The certificate corpus and cited proofs were not independently rerun.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(k\ge0\), write \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) indivisible goods. The finite nonnegative real number \(v_{ig}\) is agent \(i\)'s value for good \(g\); her value for a bundle \(S\subseteq[m]\) is \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\). A complete allocation is an ordered partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) into pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed and every good is allocated exactly once. Envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX) means that, for all agents \(i,j\) and all \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_{ig}>0\), one has \(v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\). Both the positivity test and the comparison use agent \(i\)'s valuation. If all goods in \(A_j\) have value zero for \(i\), there is no inequality for that pair. Values need not be rational or strictly positive. No payments, chores, discarded goods, randomized allocations, or efficiency requirement are present. This uses the positive-good convention of Definition 5 in the cited survey; the stronger per-allocation condition EFX-zero also tests goods with value zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence for every valuation matrix in the stated domain, or prove its negation in Lean: there are finite \(n\ge4\), \(m\ge0\), and nonnegative additive valuations for which every complete partition violates at least one of the stated EFX inequalities. The target is existence, with no algorithmic, efficiency or stronger fairness requirement.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\). The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. \(\mathrm{EFX}_{0}\) implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: Constant-factor universally truthful auctions for submodular bidders
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal:
Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and one uniform randomized combinatorial-auction mechanism with polynomial worst-case communication which is universally truthful and, for every number \(n\ge1\) of bidders, number \(m\ge1\) of items, public precision bound \(B\ge1\), and admissible normalized monotone submodular valuation profile \(v\), satisfies
\[\mathbb E_r\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i(v;r))\right]
\ \ge\ \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(v)}{C}?\]
The constant is independent of \(n,m,B\). The expectation is over report-independent mechanism randomness. For each fixed random realization the allocation and payment rule must satisfy the dominant-strategy inequality below. Communication is measured in bits, with unlimited terminating local computation and arbitrary interactive messages, including demand queries.
cards.definitions:
Items and types. Let \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Bidder \(i\) privately holds the entire function \(v_i:2^{[m]}\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). It is normalized, monotone and submodular: for all subsets \(S,T\subseteq[m]\),
\[v_i(\varnothing)=0,\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow v_i(S)\le v_i(T),\]
\[v_i(S)+v_i(T)\ge v_i(S\cup T)+v_i(S\cap T).\]
The public integer \(B\ge1\) bounds each value separately: every value admits a representation \(p/q\) with integers \(0\le p<2^B\), \(1\le q<2^B\). Write \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\) for this domain. Different bidders may have completely different functions in the domain. Their full tables have \(2^m\) entries each and are private local inputs, not publicly supplied data. There is no oracle promise, common valuation, eligibility graph, prior distribution, budget or succinct representation requirement on the types. The domain of an alternative reported valuation is also \(\mathcal V_{m,B}\), with the same public parameters.

Outcomes and utilities. A feasible allocation is \(a:[m]\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with zero meaning unallocated. Bidder \(i\) receives \(S_i=\{j:a(j)=i\}\); bundles are pairwise disjoint and no item is split. Each bidder has a finite rational payment \(p_i\in\mathbb Q\), with positive sign meaning money paid to the auctioneer. Its utility is \(v_i(S_i)-p_i\). No individual-rationality, budget-balance or transfer-sign condition is added. For a true profile \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define
\[W_v(a)=\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(S_i),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(v)=\max_{a:[m]\to\{0,\ldots,n\}}W_v(a).\]
The finite maximum exists. Welfare measures bidder values only; it excludes payments and auctioneer revenue. Zero valuations and zero optimum are allowed. All bidders are evaluated using their true values at the final allocation.

Communication model. The auctioneer and bidders run a common uniform protocol on distributed reported types. Local algorithms are ordinary finite programs, with unrestricted computation on their private tables; all local computations and protocol executions must terminate. The auctioneer initially knows only \(n,m,B\). A public blackboard holds the transcript; each transmitted bit counts once. The next speaker and the decision to halt are determined by the public transcript, public parameters and fixed random tape. Private computation time and silent delays are not messages or additional information channels. The output allocation and all payments are written to the transcript and count toward its length. Any use of private channels can instead be specified with sender and recipient information and charged in the transcript.

Rational values, prices and payments are communicated exactly as finite binary numerator/positive-denominator pairs, with a sign bit when needed and self-delimiting integer encodings. For example, for \(z\ge0\), use \(1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(z+1)\), where \(\ell\) is the bit length of \(z+1\). Subsets can be transmitted by their \(m\)-bit incidence vectors. Every query description, price, reply, routing description and final output is charged. A value query specifies a bidder and a bundle and receives its value. A demand query specifies rational item prices \((\pi_j)_{j\in[m]}\) and receives a bundle maximizing \(v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}\pi_j\). Any deterministic tie rule needed to define the mechanism is part of the protocol. Solving that finite optimization locally has no time charge, but sending its prices and answer does. These are examples of allowed messages, not an exhaustive query restriction.

Polynomial communication and randomness. There must exist constants \(K>0\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that the total number of transmitted bits is at most \(K(n+m+B+1)^d\) for every valid reported profile and every realization of the mechanism’s random bits. This is worst-case communication, not expected communication and not merely a query count. Randomness is a public tape of independent fair bits, independent of all types and reports; its use and local computation are uncharged, although execution still terminates. The uniform protocol describes how those bits are used. Fixing the tape \(r\) defines a deterministic allocation and payment rule \((S(v;r),p(v;r))\).

Universal truthfulness. For every public parameter triple, every fixed \(r\), bidder \(i\), true and alternative reported types \(v_i,w_i\in\mathcal V_{m,B}\), and other reported profile \(b_{-i}\in\mathcal V_{m,B}^{n-1}\), require
\[v_i(S_i(v_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(v_i,b_{-i};r)
\ \ge\ v_i(S_i(w_i,b_{-i};r))-p_i(w_i,b_{-i};r).\]
Both sides use the same true valuation and random tape. The protocol implements this direct-report outcome rule without transmitting the full reported tables. There is no averaging in the incentive condition; averaging is used only in the welfare guarantee. No assumption that other bidders are honest, no prior over their values, and no weakening to Bayesian or truthful-in-expectation incentives is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. A positive answer must specify the uniform protocol, payment rule and randomization, a fixed approximation constant and a fixed polynomial communication bound. Prove feasibility, termination, all-bit accounting, the incentive inequality for every fixed random tape, and the expected welfare bound for every admissible profile.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed constant and every protocol in the full model, including arbitrary interactive messages, demand queries and unlimited local computation. Failure of one mechanism or one prescribed approximation constant does not refute existence of another. A lower bound restricted to value queries, deterministic mechanisms, a particular family of allocation rules, or polynomial local time alone is insufficient.

Truthfulness in expectation alone, approximate incentives, a factor growing with \(m\), an uncharged exponential price description, or a constant guarantee with extra valuation promises does not meet the target. Conditional impossibility results must keep their hypotheses explicit and do not by themselves refute this unconditional communication claim. The target is expected welfare; a stronger high-probability guarantee is welcome but not required.

cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected general upper guarantee remains \(O((\log\log m)^2)\) with universal truthfulness and expected welfare. Value-query lower bounds do not cover arbitrary communication. The February 2026 graph-auction theorem and August procurement claims have distinct restrictions or type spaces. No matching constant-factor resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; complete cited proofs were not independently formalized.

context_blocks.text: A bidder may value several items as substitutes. For example, a coverage valuation assigns each item a set of useful features and values a bundle by the total weight of features covered at least once. Receiving an item has less marginal value when many of its features are already covered. Submodularity abstracts this diminishing-returns property without requiring the valuation to be supplied as an explicit coverage instance.

The auctioneer must allocate the items using information held by strategic bidders. Maximizing the sum of their values is the social-welfare objective; maximizing the auctioneer’s revenue would be a different problem. Payments influence what information bidders choose to provide, but are transfers and do not enter the welfare objective. Even a very poor revenue guarantee would be acceptable here if incentives and welfare met the stated requirements.

Two established results cover separate parts of the requirements. With complete reports and unrestricted resources, the Vickrey–Clarke–Groves mechanism obtains optimal welfare and truthful incentives. If incentives are omitted, submodular welfare admits constant-factor approximation from compact queries. The difficulty is combining the guarantees while avoiding communication of exponentially many bundle values. The 2026 graph-auctions paper describes this communication perspective explicitly.

Universal truthfulness is a strong use of randomization: each mechanism obtained after fixing the coins must itself make truthful reporting optimal. Truthfulness in expectation requires only that the average utility discourage lying. The distinction has mathematical force; Dobzinski and Dughmi separate the two notions in a restricted multi-unit setting. Their separation is useful background, but their multi-unit approximation scheme does not supply a mechanism for arbitrary heterogeneous submodular valuations.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. The later journal publication records the same advance, rather than a new constant-factor result. These approximation factors are asymptotic as the number of items grows.

Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla’s Theorem 2 improves the expected approximation factor for submodular and XOS bidders to \(O((\log\log m)^2)\), using at most one value or demand query per bidder. For the broader subadditive class the guarantee is \(O((\log\log m)^3)\). The theorem is universally truthful. The squared iterated logarithm still diverges, so it does not supply the fixed constant sought here.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

An August 2026 preprint claims constant budget-feasible approximations with demand queries. Its buyer purchases services from sellers with private participation costs under a payment budget. That is a different type space and objective from allocating items among bidders with private submodular bundle values. The result therefore does not resolve this card, even though both settings use truthfulness and submodularity.

A demand answer can describe a preferred bundle in \(m\) bits even if finding it requires comparing exponentially many bundles. The price vector must also be sent and paid for in the communication bound. This explains why a communication-efficient mechanism can delegate difficult optimization to a bidder without being computationally efficient for that bidder. It also explains why a bound on the number of queries alone is not a complete bit-cost specification.

Dobzinski’s impossibility theorem rules out universally truthful \(m^{1/2- \varepsilon}\)-approximation using polynomially many value queries, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). A value query reveals only one specified bundle’s value. The theorem is a genuine barrier in that access model, but it cannot be extended by simply treating a demand query as one more value query. A demand answer can encode the result of comparing exponentially many bundles.

Assadi and Singla’s FOCS 2019 result gives a universally truthful expected \(O((\log\log m)^3)\) welfare approximation with polynomially many queries. The later journal publication records the same advance, rather than a new constant-factor result. These approximation factors are asymptotic as the number of items grows.

Assadi, Kesselheim and Singla’s Theorem 2 improves the expected approximation factor for submodular and XOS bidders to \(O((\log\log m)^2)\), using at most one value or demand query per bidder. For the broader subadditive class the guarantee is \(O((\log\log m)^3)\). The theorem is universally truthful. The squared iterated logarithm still diverges, so it does not supply the fixed constant sought here.

Recent positive results for graph auctions restrict each item to a small set of eligible bidders. For example, the 2026 paper gives a truthful factor-two mechanism when each item has two eligible bidders and valuations are subadditive. This structural restriction supplies information absent in a general auction, so it does not settle the present question. A general constant-factor mechanism would show that exact incentive compatibility need not impose an unbounded welfare loss in this central communication model.

An August 2026 preprint claims constant budget-feasible approximations with demand queries. Its buyer purchases services from sellers with private participation costs under a payment budget. That is a different type space and objective from allocating items among bidders with private submodular bundle values. The result therefore does not resolve this card, even though both settings use truthfulness and submodularity.

cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Determine, with the absolute \(1/100\) acceptance precision below, the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega=\inf\{\tau\in\mathbb R:\exists C>0\ \forall n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge2\Rightarrow s(n)\le Cn^\tau\}\). Here s(n) is the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit computing all entries of the product of two arbitrary n by n complex matrices exactly, in the model below.
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge2\), the inputs are the \(2n^2\) independent complex variables \(a_{ij},b_{ij}\), with \(1\le i,j\le n\). The required n squared outputs are the polynomials \(c_{ij}=\sum_{t=1}^n a_{it}b_{tj}\). A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are input variables or constants from \(\mathbb C\), and whose other nodes have two ordered inputs and apply addition, subtraction or multiplication. Multiple uses of a previously computed value are allowed. Each ordered output position (i,j) designates a node whose polynomial is exactly c_ij, so one circuit must be correct on every pair of complex matrices. Circuit topology and constants may depend on n, but not on the matrix entries. Size is the number of arithmetic gates, including gates operating on constants; source nodes and output designations have zero cost. No division, comparison, branching, randomness, approximation or test of the input values is permitted. This is a nonuniform algebraic model: a separate finite circuit may be chosen for each n, with no required algorithm generating the circuits or their constants. Scalar arithmetic is exact, and costs of representing complex numbers in bits are outside the model. The number of gates differs only by a constant factor from the source’s binary-circuit wire measure, and allowing an explicit subtraction gate also changes size by at most a constant factor; neither changes the exponent. Define s(n) as the least size among correct circuits. This minimum exists because the elementary multiplication formula gives a circuit, and sizes are nonnegative integers. The n squared output polynomials are distinct and none is a source polynomial, so each needs a distinct arithmetic gate and \(s(n)\ge n^2\). The elementary upper bound \(s(n)\le2n^3\) makes the exponent set nonempty and gives \(2\le\omega\le3\). The infimum need not be attained. Specifically, \(\omega\le u\) means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a real \(C_\varepsilon>0\) such that \(s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{u+\varepsilon}\) for every integer n at least two. A lower bound \(\omega\ge\ell\) means that for every real \(\tau<\ell\) and C>0 there is an integer n at least two with \(s(n)>Cn^\tau\). These quantified bounds do not demand a circuit family attaining the endpoint exponent or a pointwise lower bound at that endpoint. The source’s conjecture \(\omega=2\) is one possible value of the numerical target selected for this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real number a by an unambiguous mathematical description and give a complete Lean-checked proof that \(|a-\omega|\le1/100\) for the unrestricted circuit quantity above. Equivalently, certify bounds \(\ell\le\omega\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) and take \(a=(\ell+u)/2\). A proved exact value also qualifies. The proof must justify both sides of the error interval, with the infimum and nonattainment conventions in the definitions. Merely copying or renaming the defining infimum, reporting an optimized upper bound, or giving a bound only for a restricted tensor method does not meet the requirement. This tolerance concerns the value of the exponent and does not assert a proof of the exact conjecture that omega equals two.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes \(n^{2}\) inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent \(\log _{2}7\).

The scientific target is the value of the exponent, whether it equals two or is larger. The familiar \(\omega =2\) conjecture specifies one possible answer. Because \(\omega\) is an infimum, an upper bound may approach it with a different circuit family and constant for every positive slack in the exponent. Exact scalar arithmetic over a fixed field separates this quantity from approximate numerical multiplication and hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

Alman proves a lower bound of 2.16805 for exponents achievable by applying the universal method to Coppersmith–Winograd tensors. That bound quantifies over a specified tensor framework. It does not imply \(\omega\ge2.16805\), because the quantity in this card permits every arithmetic circuit over the complex numbers.

An improvement in an upper bound and a determination of the exponent are different achievements. Even the reported upper bound 2.371177, together with the elementary lower bound 2, leaves an interval much wider than the required 0.02. A certified value within 0.01 would locate the optimum more closely, while still not necessarily deciding the exact conjecture \(\omega=2\).
