cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.
cards.why: This is the central equality question for general arithmetic computation. It asks whether a polynomial-size algebraic computation can always absorb a sum over exponentially many Boolean witnesses, with the permanent serving as a complete concrete target. A separation would establish a general limitation despite arbitrary constants, cancellations and reuse; equality would give polynomial-size circuits for every polynomial family in VNP.

The August OpenAI chapter reports a general permanent lower bound of order n^2 log log n and formula lower bounds, with released Lean certificates; these remain polynomial and the certificates were not independently replayed here. context_blocks.text: The permanent of a matrix sums the weights of its perfect matchings when rows and columns form the two sides of a bipartite graph. For a zero-one matrix it counts perfect matchings. Already in dimension two, \(\operatorname{perm}_2(X)=x_{11}x_{22}+x_{12}x_{21}\), while the determinant subtracts the second product. This card concerns the symbolic polynomial for all complex inputs.

The determinant contains the same permutation products with signs, yet has polynomial-size division-free circuits. Thus factorially many displayed terms do not force factorial circuit size. Reusing expressions and canceling terms are central powers of the model. Counting perfect matchings on binary inputs is a related Boolean counting problem, but that bit-complexity problem is not the same as allowing arbitrary complex constants at unit arithmetic cost.

Valiant’s completeness theorem makes the permanent universal for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over fields of characteristic different from two. Each VNP family can be obtained from a polynomially larger permanent by substituting variables and field constants. This establishes the equivalence in the question over \(\mathbb C\). The field choice matters: in characteristic two the permanent and determinant coincide.

Ryser’s identity gives an exponential-size upper bound, including formulas using \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations. In contrast, a positive answer here requires one fixed polynomial bound for all dimensions. A formula is a circuit whose intermediate results cannot be shared; forbidding reuse can substantially increase the needed size.

Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for every constant circuit depth over characteristic-zero fields. Their hard polynomial is an iterated matrix product entry, which itself has polynomial-size unrestricted circuits. The low-depth theorem therefore illustrates the power of removing a depth restriction rather than proving VP different from VNP. The result first appeared in 2021 and was published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.

The 1 August 2026 OpenAI manuscript reports a lower bound \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) for unrestricted division-free circuits computing the permanent, and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) for formulas, including formulas with valid divisions. The circuit model in Chapter 5 matches this card, but the bound is still polynomial in matrix dimension and hence does not separate VP and VNP. The release supplies Lean certificates; this review checked the mathematical statements and repository description without replaying or independently auditing those certificates.

Narayanan’s work, published on ECCC on 9 August 2026 after a July submission, reports improved superlinear lower bounds for certain sublogarithmic depths and explicit elusive curves of exponential degree. The manuscript explicitly explains that its current parameters do not establish VP different from VNP. These are results with stated depth and degree qualifications, not a general superpolynomial permanent lower bound.

A determinantal representation expresses a polynomial as \(\det A(x)\), where every matrix entry is an affine linear form in its variables. Its minimum matrix dimension measures a more restricted representation than an arbitrary arithmetic circuit. A superpolynomial bound on that dimension alone does not settle this card; polynomial-size general circuits can be simulated by determinantal representations of quasipolynomial size. Exact representation must also be distinguished from taking limits of such representations.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint gives deterministic polynomial bit-time approximation of the permanent of nonnegative rational matrices within a factor \(\exp(O(n(\log\log n)^2/\log n))\). This is a recent algorithmic advance for numerical approximate counting. Its input restriction and multiplicative-error guarantee do not give exact formal-polynomial circuits over \(\mathbb C\).

cards.context:
The permanent of a matrix sums the weights of its perfect matchings when rows and columns form the two sides of a bipartite graph. For a zero-one matrix it counts perfect matchings. Already in dimension two, \(\operatorname{perm}_2(X)=x_{11}x_{22}+x_{12}x_{21}\), while the determinant subtracts the second product. This card concerns the symbolic polynomial for all complex inputs.

The determinant contains the same permutation products with signs, yet has polynomial-size division-free circuits. Thus factorially many displayed terms do not force factorial circuit size. Reusing expressions and canceling terms are central powers of the model. Counting perfect matchings on binary inputs is a related Boolean counting problem, but that bit-complexity problem is not the same as allowing arbitrary complex constants at unit arithmetic cost.

Valiant’s completeness theorem makes the permanent universal for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over fields of characteristic different from two. Each VNP family can be obtained from a polynomially larger permanent by substituting variables and field constants. This establishes the equivalence in the question over \(\mathbb C\). The field choice matters: in characteristic two the permanent and determinant coincide.

Ryser’s identity gives an exponential-size upper bound, including formulas using \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations. In contrast, a positive answer here requires one fixed polynomial bound for all dimensions. A formula is a circuit whose intermediate results cannot be shared; forbidding reuse can substantially increase the needed size.

Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for every constant circuit depth over characteristic-zero fields. Their hard polynomial is an iterated matrix product entry, which itself has polynomial-size unrestricted circuits. The low-depth theorem therefore illustrates the power of removing a depth restriction rather than proving VP different from VNP. The result first appeared in 2021 and was published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.

The 1 August 2026 OpenAI manuscript reports a lower bound \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) for unrestricted division-free circuits computing the permanent, and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) for formulas, including formulas with valid divisions. The circuit model in Chapter 5 matches this card, but the bound is still polynomial in matrix dimension and hence does not separate VP and VNP. The release supplies Lean certificates; this review checked the mathematical statements and repository description without replaying or independently auditing those certificates.

Narayanan’s work, published on ECCC on 9 August 2026 after a July submission, reports improved superlinear lower bounds for certain sublogarithmic depths and explicit elusive curves of exponential degree. The manuscript explicitly explains that its current parameters do not establish VP different from VNP. These are results with stated depth and degree qualifications, not a general superpolynomial permanent lower bound.

A determinantal representation expresses a polynomial as \(\det A(x)\), where every matrix entry is an affine linear form in its variables. Its minimum matrix dimension measures a more restricted representation than an arbitrary arithmetic circuit. A superpolynomial bound on that dimension alone does not settle this card; polynomial-size general circuits can be simulated by determinantal representations of quasipolynomial size. Exact representation must also be distinguished from taking limits of such representations.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint gives deterministic polynomial bit-time approximation of the permanent of nonnegative rational matrices within a factor \(\exp(O(n(\log\log n)^2/\log n))\). This is a recent algorithmic advance for numerical approximate counting. Its input restriction and multiplicative-error guarantee do not give exact formal-polynomial circuits over \(\mathbb C\).

benchmark_focus.reason: This is the central equality question for general arithmetic computation. It asks whether a polynomial-size algebraic computation can always absorb a sum over exponentially many Boolean witnesses, with the permanent serving as a complete concrete target. A separation would establish a general limitation despite arbitrary constants, cancellations and reuse; equality would give polynomial-size circuits for every polynomial family in VNP.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine \(A\) that, on every input encoding a polynomial \(f\in\mathbb Z[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\) with \(m\geq1\), halts and outputs YES exactly when \[\exists(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m\quad f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0,\] and outputs NO otherwise? The number of variables, degree and coefficients are unrestricted finite input data, and there is no time or space efficiency requirement.
cards.definitions:
The field \(\mathbb Q\) consists of exact fractions \(a/b\), with \(a\in\mathbb Z\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), identifying fractions of the same value; addition and multiplication are the usual exact field operations. A polynomial input describes \(f=\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_j\prod_{i=1}^{m}X_i^{e_{ji}}\), with \(r\geq0\), \(a_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(e_{ji}\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Repeated monomials and zero coefficients are allowed. The empty sum is the zero polynomial and \(X_i^0=1\), including when evaluating at zero. Constants are represented with all exponents zero. A rational zero is any tuple in \(\mathbb Q^m\) giving exact value zero; there is no bound on its numerators or denominators and no integrality restriction.

Use the following explicit effective binary encoding. For \(u\geq0\), let \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^b0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(b\) bits and no leading zeroes. Encode an integer \(a\) by a sign bit followed by \(\operatorname{code}(|a|)\), with 0 denoting a nonnegative integer and 1 a negative integer; negative zero is invalid. A complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(m)\operatorname{code}(r)\), followed for each \(j=1,\ldots,r\) by the signed code of \(a_j\) and \(\operatorname{code}(e_{j1}),\ldots,\operatorname{code}(e_{jm})\), with no trailing bits. Require \(m\geq1\). The machine halts and outputs NO on every malformed encoding.

The algorithm is a single finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program with a finite tape alphabet, ordinary discrete transitions and unbounded work tapes, without advice or an oracle. On every input it must halt after finitely many transitions; its running time need not satisfy a polynomial, elementary or other prescribed bound. Its program is independent of \(m,r\), all degrees and all coefficients. The input supplies only the polynomial, without additional height-comparison predicates or a promise of solvability. The question concerns decision of existence; a YES output need not itself contain a rational tuple.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of the existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must specify one effective algorithm and prove termination and exact correctness on every polynomial in the stated domain, together with rejection of invalid input. A negative answer must prove that no such total correct Turing machine exists. Recognizing only polynomials that have a rational zero, excluding polynomial-time algorithms, or proving undecidability for equations with integer-constrained unknowns or added predicates does not establish the required negation. Any conditional result must be identified as conditional and does not alone settle this unconditional question.
cards.why: This asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver. It connects the computability of arithmetic, logical definability and the existence of rational points on algebraic varieties. The unresolved boundary persists despite undecidability over the integers and decidability of polynomial feasibility over the reals and algebraically closed fields; allowing fractions fundamentally changes the permitted witnesses.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be effectively enumerated and tested by exact substitution, so every YES-instance is eventually recognizable. Such a search does not halt on a NO-instance. The target requires termination in both cases, irrespective of efficiency. A solver for all instances would also allow a rational zero to be found when one exists.

The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem proves that no general algorithm decides integer solvability. It does not automatically decide the rational problem: \(2X-1=0\) has a rational zero but no integer zero. A rational solver cannot simply be applied to the unchanged integer equation.

Allowing rational coefficients gives the same decision problem, because their denominators can be cleared effectively. Finite systems of equations are also equivalent to a single equation: over \(\mathbb Q\), \(f_1=\cdots=f_r=0\) holds exactly when \(\sum_i f_i^2=0\). More generally, disequalities can be encoded using inverse variables and disjunctions using products. These equivalences identify the problem with decidability of the existential first-order theory of \(\mathbb Q\) in the language of rings.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathbb Q\) would transfer integer undecidability to this problem. Koenigsmann’s Theorem 1 instead defines \(\mathbb Z\) by a universal formula; its Corollary 3 establishes undecidability for universal-existential sentences. Quantifier alternation is essential to that conclusion: the full first-order theory and the universal-existential fragment are already undecidable, while neither fact settles the purely existential target.

Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman prove undecidability over the ring of integers \(\mathcal O_K\) of every number field \(K\). Here a number field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb Q\), and \(\mathcal O_K\) consists of elements satisfying a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. This restricts the solution domain; in particular \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Z\), whereas the present question permits every rational number.

Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the recent proof of undecidability for these rings and supplies an alternative definability argument from rank stability. Its Theorem 4.2 concerns definitions over rings of integers. This account does not extend the negative answer to the whole field \(\mathbb Q\).

Garcia-Fritz, Pasten and Vidaux prove undecidability when rational equations are supplemented with finitely many height-comparison conditions. For a rational tuple \(q\), their logarithmic height is \(h(q)=\log\max\{d,|dq_1|,\ldots,|dq_m|\}\), where \(d\geq1\) is its least common denominator, and the added predicates compare heights of tuples. These extra constraints are absent from the target. Their ordinary rational-solvability question remains explicitly open.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.
Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal:
Determine the optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance function
\[R_2(\delta)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)}{n},\qquad 0<\delta<\frac12,\]
where \(A_2(n,d)\) is the largest cardinality of any nonempty binary code of length \(n\) whose distinct codewords have Hamming distance at least \(d\). Supply an unambiguous real-valued approximation \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\), with a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall\delta\in(0,1/2),\qquad |g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The error is absolute rate error in information bits per transmitted bit. Codes may be nonlinear and have no construction, encoding or decoding efficiency requirement. The same error bound must hold on the entire real domain.
cards.definitions:
Finite codes. For integers \(n\ge1\) and \(0\le d\le n\), a binary length-\(n\) code is a nonempty subset \(C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n\). Its elements are codewords. For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}^n\), define their Hamming distance by
\[d_H(x,y)=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\ne y_i\}|.\]
The distance requirement means \(d_H(x,y)\ge d\) for every distinct pair \(x,y\in C\). A singleton satisfies it vacuously; no minimum over an empty set needs to be chosen. Define
\[A_2(n,d)=\max\{|C|:\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ \forall x,y\in C,\ x\ne y\Rightarrow d_H(x,y)\ge d\}.\]
This is a finite maximum over a nonempty collection, and \(1\le A_2(n,d)\le2^n\). The rate of \(C\) is \(r(C)=\log_2|C|/n\). The distance parameter \(d/n\) is a required relative separation, not the fraction of independent random channel errors. All logarithms are base two.

Asymptotic convention. Fix the real parameter \(\delta\) before taking the block length to infinity. The integer \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\) is the smallest integer at least \(\delta n\). For \(0\le\delta\le1\), write \(a_n(\delta)=\log_2 A_2(n,\lceil\delta n\rceil)/n\). Explicitly,
\[R_2(\delta)=\inf_{N\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\ \sup_{n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge N} a_n(\delta).\]
Every term is in \([0,1]\), so the tail suprema and infimum are well-defined finite real numbers. The limsup allows a favorable infinite subsequence of block lengths and does not assert that the ordinary limit exists. The optimum ranges over all codes, without linearity or a single effective code-family generator. The requested domain is exactly \((0,1/2)\); the same definition outside it gives the known regimes \(R_2(0)=1\) and \(R_2(\delta)=0\) for \(1/2\le\delta\le1\).

Conventions for bounds. A lower curve \(L\) satisfies \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\), every \(\varepsilon>0\) and every integer \(N\ge1\), there are an integer \(n\ge N\) and a valid code of length \(n\), distance at least \(\lceil\delta n\rceil\), and rate at least \(L(\delta)-\varepsilon\). An upper curve \(U\) satisfies \(R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) precisely when, for each fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), some integer \(N\ge1\) has the following property: for every \(n\ge N\), every valid code at that distance has rate at most \(U(\delta)+\varepsilon\). Block length thresholds may depend on \(\delta\) and \(\varepsilon\); a common threshold for all real distances is not required. These existence bounds do not impose polynomial-time code construction.

For the background bounds, the binary entropy is \(h_2(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t)\) on \([0,1]\), with each endpoint term \(0\log_2 0\) interpreted as zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified function \(g:(0,1/2)\to\mathbb R\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(|g(\delta)-R_2(\delta)|\le1/100\) for every real \(\delta\) in that domain, using the finite-code maximum, rounding, limsup and normalization above. This requires both \(g(\delta)-1/100\le R_2(\delta)\) and \(R_2(\delta)\le g(\delta)+1/100\); the preceding quantified code statements specify the corresponding lower and upper guarantees. Alternatively, certified curves \(L,U\) satisfying \(L(\delta)\le R_2(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) everywhere qualify through their midpoint. A formula, certified evaluation rule or another unambiguous mathematical description may specify the answer; no predetermined formula grammar or evaluation-time bound is imposed. Merely renaming the defining optimization or limsup does not supply the requested determination. An exact determination qualifies, but exact equality to the Gilbert–Varshamov curve is not required. Finitely many samples, an uncertified numerical plot, a bound on only one side, or a result restricted to linear codes or to some distances does not establish the stated whole-domain guarantee.
cards.why: This function is the intrinsic packing limit for binary information protected against worst-case substitutions. Determining it to a certified rate accuracy would quantify the necessary redundancy independently of how a code is represented, constructed or decoded. Exact determination would settle a foundational coding-theory question; the selected tolerance is a distinct, weaker benchmark target.

context_blocks.text: A code represents messages by selected bit strings. More codewords carry more information per transmitted bit, while greater pairwise separation permits correction of more adversarial errors. This question asks for the best possible asymptotic compromise over every binary code, independently of algorithmic restrictions.

The repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, and corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The complete set of three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, and cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. In general, correction of every pattern of at most \(t\) substitutions requires and is guaranteed by pairwise distance at least \(2t+1\), for an integer \(t\ge0\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov existence bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\ge1-h_2(\delta)\), whereas the elementary Hamming bound gives \(R_2(\delta)\le1-h_2(\delta/2)\). Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.9 asks for the largest asymptotically attainable binary rate at a fixed relative distance. Its infinite-family formulation is represented here by the explicit limsup and subsequence convention.

The 1977 McEliece–Rodemich–Rumsey–Welch bounds sharpen the upper side. The first gives \(R_2(\delta)\le h_2(1/2-\sqrt{\delta(1-\delta)})\); the second is never weaker. These were the long-standing general upper bounds, but the August 2026 preprints report strict improvements, so the 1977 frontier must not be described as current.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s 10 August 2026 preprint reports strict improvements to the first and second MRRW bounds at every \(0<\delta<1/2\). The theorems concern arbitrary classical binary codes, including nonlinear ones; quantum states occur in the analysis and do not change the code alphabet. The introduction still identifies the GV curve as the best general asymptotic lower bound.

The requested tolerance needs a separate check from exact openness. At relative distance one quarter, the GV rate is approximately 0.18872, while Table 2 of the August preprint reports a numerical upper-bound estimate near 0.35038. The authors explicitly label the table as floating-point evaluations, not certified global optima. These reported values illustrate the remaining difference between the displayed lower and upper estimates; they are not a certified interval or a proof that no different approximation theorem exists. The checked sources do not supply the requested error of 0.01 throughout the domain.

Barg’s 1 September 2026 note compares the new channel bound with the concurrent Delsarte-certificate result. Its Section 2 identifies the coinciding variational formulas for the improvement of the first MRRW bound. The note provides a mathematical relation between those results, rather than a determination of the full rate–distance function.

Finite-length improvements can leave the limiting rate unchanged. Jiang and Vardy obtain a factor of order \(n\) over the binary Gilbert bound for each fixed \(0<\delta\le0.499\). Such a multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log n/n)\) after taking the logarithm and dividing by block length. It does not constitute an increase in the asymptotic rate exponent.

Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a probabilistic proof of a square-root block-length improvement for linear codes and an extension to quantum codes. The paper acknowledges the earlier classical square-root improvement. These polynomial factors do not by themselves alter \(R_2\), and the quantum-code statement has different objects and constraints.

Capacity under independent random bit flips, list decoding, and codes over larger alphabets have different targets. This card asks for worst-case pairwise separation over the binary alphabet. A construction above the GV curve at even one distance would address the separate beyond-GV question, while this card requires two-sided accuracy over the entire distance interval.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal:
Determine the weighted capacity function
\[F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for all \(a,b\in\mathbb R\), \(P_{1},P_{2}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). The real memoryless channel is
\[Y_{1,t}=X_{1,t}+aX_{2,t}+Z_{1,t},\qquad Y_{2,t}=bX_{1,t}+X_{2,t}+Z_{2,t}.\]
The region \(C\) uses two independent private messages, deterministic separate encoders, average power over messages and time, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing joint average decoding error, as defined below. The required absolute accuracy is \(1/100\) bit per real channel use everywhere on this domain.
cards.definitions:
All five parameters are finite real numbers and remain fixed as block length grows. Negative, zero, and positive gains are included; powers may be zero or arbitrarily large. The two direct gains and the noise variances are normalized to one. For every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and time \(t\), the noise \(Z_{i,t}\) has density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-z^{2}/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). All these noises are mutually independent and independent of both messages. There is no fading, channel state, or additional channel memory. Channel parameters and both codebooks are known to all terminals.

For a positive integer \(K\), let \([K]=\{0,\ldots,K-1\}\). An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code has \(n,K_{1},K_{2}\ge1\), two independent uniform messages \(M_{i}\in[K_{i}]\), deterministic encoders \(f_{i}:[K_{i}]\to\mathbb R^{n}\), and Borel-measurable decoders \(d_{i}:\mathbb R^{n}\to[K_{i}]\). Transmitter \(i\) sends \(X_{i}^{n}=f_{i}(M_{i})\), and receiver \(i\) estimates only its own message using \(d_{i}(Y_{i}^{n})\). Each code must satisfy
\[\frac{1}{nK_{i}}\sum_{m\in[K_{i}]}\sum_{t=1}^{n}f_{i}(m)_{t}^{2}\le P_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
This is a separate power budget for each transmitter, averaged over messages and time. It is not a bound on every symbol or every individual codeword, and power cannot be transferred between transmitters. The error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y_{1}^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Y_{2}^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
averaged over the independent uniform messages and all Gaussian noise. There is no maximal-error-over-messages requirement. The encoders may depend arbitrarily on time and their own messages, with arbitrary real codeword entries and no computation bound. They have no shared random seed, common message, feedback, or communication link; neither encoder knows the other message. The receivers cannot communicate. Predetermined time sharing, unequal powers in different phases, and arbitrary temporal dependence within each codeword are allowed subject to the displayed average budgets. There is no secrecy or prescribed signaling-distribution constraint.

All rate logarithms have base two. A nonnegative rate pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a code for each integer block length \(n\ge1\), with message sizes \(K_{i,n}\), such that \(P_{e,n}\to0\) and
\[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_{2}K_{i,n}}{n}\ge R_{i},\qquad i=1,2.\]
The region \(C(a,b,P_{1},P_{2})\) is the Euclidean closure of all achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\), where \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\); hence \(F\) is finite. These are bits per one real scalar channel use, not per complex channel use. No finite block code must attain a boundary rate. The weights include both endpoints, and the exact supporting function determines the closed region. The task has real mathematical parameters; it does not silently restrict them or the codebooks to rational encodings.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on \(\mathbb R^{2}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\times[0,1]\) and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that, for every tuple in this domain,
\[|g(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)-F(a,b,P_{1},P_{2},\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must justify both sides of this error against the operational code definition, using its average-power and average-error conventions and bits per real use. Certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) qualify by their midpoint. An exact function also qualifies. A formula or another unambiguous mathematical description may be used; no single-letter syntax, fixed number of auxiliary variables, polynomial evaluation bound, or finite encoding of arbitrary real inputs is required. Any proposed evaluation rule must have a proved meaning and the stated guarantee on the full real domain. An unevaluated restatement of the capacity optimization or its limiting code definition, a sampled plot, and bounds with an unclosed gap do not determine the answer. Sum capacity alone, a restricted signaling optimum, a special interference regime, or an asymptotic high-power approximation is insufficient. The fixed tolerance does not assert an exact capacity theorem.

context_blocks.text: Two separately informed transmitters use the same medium, so each receiver observes its desired signal plus interference and Gaussian noise. The point-to-point rate \(c_{i}=\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{i})\) is an individual upper bound, but the two upper bounds generally cannot be reached together. The target describes every tradeoff between the independent conversations; knowing only their best total rate leaves other supporting weights undetermined.

The general two-user model is a foundational network information theory problem. Han–Kobayashi regions are established achievable inner bounds, and several structured parameter regimes have exact capacity or exact sum-capacity results. Shang and Chen’s monograph explicitly distinguishes these two kinds of conclusions. An optimal value within one specified signaling family is also different from a converse bounding every permitted code.

For strong interference, \(|a|\ge1\) and \(|b|\ge1\), the known capacity region is given by \(0\le R_{i}\le c_{i}\) and
\[R_{1}+R_{2}\le\min\!\left\{\tfrac12\log_{2}(1+P_{1}+a^{2}P_{2}),\ \tfrac12\log_{2}(1+b^{2}P_{1}+P_{2})\right\}.\]
These are the two Gaussian multiple-access sum bounds in this card’s real normalization. With \(a=b=0\), capacity is the rectangle \([0,c_{1}]\times[0,c_{2}]\). The solved cases explain why an answer must retain both gains and both powers, rather than assume symmetry or a single interference-strength ordering.

Etkin, Tse and Wang establish the celebrated universal one-bit approximation using achievable and outer regions. The checked preprint’s formal model is complex-valued, and its error notion is an additive coordinate gap, not a bound on the error of a plotted sum-rate curve. That constant-gap theorem is a major approximate characterization, but it is not a certificate at this card’s much smaller tolerance in bits per real use. Its units and power convention must be accounted for in any precise transfer to this model.

Nair and Ng prove that allowing temporally correlated vector Gaussian inputs in the multiletter Han–Kobayashi region gives the same region as scalar Gaussian inputs when the comparison includes time sharing and its power allocation. This is an invariance theorem within a signaling class. It does not rule out other input distributions or establish full capacity. Huleihel and Merhav’s older preprint claiming an improvement from Gaussian memory was withdrawn in April 2018; its original abstract must not be counted as a valid advance.

Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 work settles a structural conjecture about the Gaussian-signaling region for the one-sided, or Z, channel. Under its explicit parameter condition, multiplexing is unnecessary for the optimum of that inner region. The theorem does not assert that the inner region equals capacity for all Z channels.

Their January 2026 manuscript gives parameters where non-Gaussian distributions outperform Gaussian ones in a restricted single-phase superposition region without power control. Its Conjecture 1 still concerns the full Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region including power allocation over time. Section II.D explains that the new counterexample regime is disjoint from the regime in which the previous no-multiplexing theorem applies. Thus these results do not jointly yield a counterexample to the full capacity conjecture. Remark 2 also records the authors’ inability to verify parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim.

Gohari, Nair and Zhao’s February 2026 manuscript combines converse bounds through auxiliary receivers. The full Gaussian discussion in Section II.C restricts its matching corner, sum-rate and slope conclusions to the stated very-weak-interference regime and corresponding one-sided specializations. These conclusions must not be expanded to arbitrary weak interference merely from the broader abstract wording. The paper supplies an outer bound, not the general capacity function.

Khandani’s current v12, posted on 7 September 2026, claims that Gaussian Han–Kobayashi signaling attains weak-interference capacity with at most two time-sharing phases. Its equations use nonnegative squared cross-gain parameters under square roots; those symbols are not this card’s possibly signed amplitude gains. Sections 7–8 present the claimed converse and optimality conclusion. This review checked that statement and scope but did not establish the correctness of the full proof for unrestricted codes. Nair–Zhao’s January criticism predates this revision and is not automatically a refutation of it. The claim covers a major subdomain and is recorded under uncertain status, without asserting a solution over all real gains.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.

context_blocks.text: Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.

cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: Is every polynomially testable property of finite simple graphs also polynomially estimable in the dense graph model? Precisely, for every graph property \(\mathcal P=(\mathcal P_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the definitions below, does existence of a uniform randomized tester and integers \(C,a\ge1\) with worst-case adjacency-query bound \(Ct^a\) imply existence of a uniform randomized distance estimator and integers \(D,b\ge1\) with bound \(Dt^b\)? The guarantees must hold for every graph order \(n\), every integer \(t\ge2\), and every input graph, with proximity and additive accuracy \(\varepsilon=1/t\). Programs and polynomial constants may depend on \(\mathcal P\), but not on \(n,t\) or the input graph.
cards.definitions: A finite simple graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is an undirected graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For each integer \(n\ge1\), \(\mathcal P_n\) is a nonempty collection of these graphs invariant under every permutation of \([n]\). No closure under vertex or edge deletion is assumed. For \(n\ge2\), define \[d(G,\mathcal P_n)=\frac{1}{\binom n2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_n}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|.\] Here \(E(G)\) is the edge set and symmetric difference \(\triangle\) counts each added or deleted edge once. Set \(d(G,\mathcal P_1)=0\). The minimum exists because \(\mathcal P_n\) is nonempty and finite. Distance lies in \([0,1]\); it is normalized by all possible unordered pairs, not by the number of present edges. A tester receives \(n,t\) in binary and can query whether any chosen pair of distinct vertices is an edge. Queries may depend on previous answers and independent fair random bits. It accepts each \(G\in\mathcal P_n\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects each \(G\) with \(d(G,\mathcal P_n)\ge1/t\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either answer is permitted when \(0<d(G,\mathcal P_n)<1/t\). An estimator has the same input and oracle access and outputs a binary-encoded rational number \(z\) such that \[\Pr\bigl[|z-d(G,\mathcal P_n)|\le1/t\bigr]\ge2/3\] on every graph, with no distance promise. Each algorithm is one finite probabilistic Turing oracle program with no advice or additional oracle. It must terminate on every execution. Local computation, storage and output length have no quantitative bound; the charged resource is the total number of adjacency queries, bounded on every input and every random execution. Each probability is over the program's random bits for the fixed input graph. The algorithm does not receive a description of \(\mathcal P\): its fixed program may depend on that property. The implication asks for existence of the estimator, not a uniform meta-algorithm taking a tester's code as input. Accuracy is required at every reciprocal integer; this discretization fixes the parameter encoding without imposing a graph-size-dependent bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal implication or of its logical negation. An affirmative proof must provide the full estimator guarantees whenever the tester hypothesis holds. A negative proof must establish a property with a polynomial-query tester for which every uniform estimator fails every fixed polynomial query bound under the same model. A separation between particular algorithms, or a conversion with exponential rather than polynomial query overhead, is insufficient. This is a yes/no question about algorithms at arbitrarily small accuracy, not a request for one distance estimate at the numerical benchmark tolerance.
cards.why: A decision tester recognizes only a large violation, whereas a distance estimator measures the minimum repair needed at every distance scale. A general polynomial implication would transfer efficient sampling guarantees to quantitative assessment across the dense-graph model. A separating property would establish an information-cost distinction between these two basic tasks even when unlimited local computation is allowed.

context_blocks.text: A tester can answer arbitrarily on inputs that are close to a property but do not satisfy it. A distance estimator must still provide an accurate number there. For example, its output must distinguish small, moderate and large repair costs on the same scale, rather than merely certify a sufficiently large violation.

The input contains \(\binom n2\) potential edge bits. A polynomial-in-\(t\) query bound is independent of \(n\), so for large graphs the algorithm reads only a small part of the adjacency relation. This is an information constraint; difficult computation on the observed sample is not excluded.

The existing card explicitly selected the polynomial implication from the stronger quantitative question in the source. Problem 5.4 asks for a conversion preserving an arbitrary testing complexity after polynomial rescaling of accuracy. Such a conversion would imply this card, but a proof of this card would not by itself establish that stronger relationship for nonpolynomial testing functions. The present review preserves this previously recorded target.

The source defines estimation through tolerance thresholds. Returning an additive-distance estimate, as used here and by Fiat–Ron, captures the polynomial-query regime as well: a polynomial number of threshold comparisons at finer accuracy, with amplified success probabilities, suffices to obtain a distance estimate. The factor between pair-count and squared-order normalization is bounded for every order at least two.

The general Fischer–Newman theorem establishes qualitative tester-to-estimator conversion. Its original quantitative loss is of tower type. This does not yield a polynomial estimator from a polynomial tester.

The later conversion improves that loss to double exponential for general properties and to single exponential for hereditary properties. Hereditary means closed under taking induced subgraphs; the universal target here has no such restriction.

Polynomial estimators are known for several particular graph classes, including the stated induced-path and chordal examples. They show that the stronger task can be efficient, but do not settle its cost for every polynomially testable graph property.

cards.title: Private PAC sample complexity from VC and Littlestone dimensions
cards.formal: Do there exist universal integers \(A,k\ge1\) such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\) on a nonempty finite domain \(\mathcal X\), with \(v=\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal C)\ge1\) and \(d=\operatorname{LD}(\mathcal C)\ge1\), has a positive integer sample size \[m\le A\bigl(1+v+\log^{*}d\bigr)^{k}\] and a possibly improper learner \(L\) that is \((1,1/(100m^{2}))\)-differentially private and realizes the following PAC guarantee? For every distribution \(D\) on \(\mathcal X\) and every target \(h^{*}\in\mathcal C\), when \(L\) receives \(m\) independent samples \((x_i,h^{*}(x_i))\) with \(x_i\sim D\), its output \(\widehat h\) satisfies \[\Pr\!\left[\Pr_{x\sim D}[\widehat h(x)\ne h^{*}(x)]\le1/10\right]\ge9/10.\] The same \(m,L\) must work for all \(D,h^{*}\) for the chosen class. Their choice can depend on the complete class, but \(A,k\) cannot. Computation is unrestricted. This is the previously selected concrete polynomial-overhead version of the source question; the constant accuracy, confidence and sample-dependent privacy parameters are editorial specifications, not parameter values asserted in the source.
cards.why: The theorem characterizing whether private learning is possible leaves an enormous quantitative gap. This question asks whether the extra data needed for privacy is controlled by ordinary statistical complexity and an exceptionally slowly growing function of sequential complexity. A positive answer would put a uniform bound on that privacy overhead across all finite concept classes.

context_blocks.text: Nonprivate PAC learning at constant accuracy and confidence has sample complexity governed by VC dimension. Approximate private learnability instead has a qualitative connection to finite Littlestone dimension. This equivalence says that a finite sample bound exists; it does not identify how large the bound must be.

The proposed bound depends polynomially on \(v\) and \(\log^{*}d\), so replacing \(d\) by another fixed power does not answer it. Yan proves a nearly matching iterated-logarithmic bound when \(v=1\), including an improper learner and explicit parameter dependence. The card retains the earlier editorial normalization \(\varepsilon=1\), error \(1/10\), failure probability \(1/10\), and \(\delta=1/(100m^{2})\). In particular, \(\delta\) is tied to the actual sample size, rather than silently treated as a fixed constant while \(m\) grows. The source suppresses these parameters, so its displayed summary bounds are context rather than claims that every hidden factor is independent of this normalization.

cards.definitions: A concept is a binary function; the learner knows \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension \(v\) is the largest cardinality of a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X\) on which the restrictions of \(\mathcal C\) realize every binary labeling. A complete binary tree of depth \(r\) has an instance point at each internal node and its two outgoing edges labeled 0 and 1. It is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is produced by one fixed concept on that path's instance points. The Littlestone dimension \(d\) is the greatest shattered depth. For \(z\ge1\), \(\log^{*}z\) is the least number of successive base-two logarithms needed to obtain a value at most one; in particular \(\log^{*}1=0\). The dimension-zero case is excluded only to avoid a logarithm convention: on a fixed nonempty domain such a class contains a single distinct concept and has a data-independent exact predictor. A learner is an arbitrary probability kernel from \((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\) to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{\mathcal X}\). It need not return a member of \(\mathcal C\). For every pair of labeled sample lists \(S,S'\) differing at one position and every subset \(E\) of output hypotheses, require \[\Pr[L(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[L(S')\in E]+1/(100m^{2}).\] Privacy holds even on samples not realizable by the class. The sample size is chosen before the target and distribution; the probability in the PAC guarantee includes both independently drawn examples and the learner's randomness. There are no runtime or representation bounds, and no uniform program across classes is required. The integer-power bound is equivalent to an unspecified universal polynomial in \(1+v\) and \(1+\log^{*}d\). A finite class on an arbitrary domain can be reduced to the finite domain of distinct label vectors \((h(x))_{h\in\mathcal C}\), of which there are at most \(2^{|\mathcal C|}\); both dimensions and these unrestricted learning/privacy requirements are preserved. Thus the finite-domain convention introduces no additional sample-complexity restriction on finite classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the universal polynomial bound or its logical negation under the exact privacy and PAC conventions above. A positive answer must supply, for every class, a sample size and private learner satisfying the guarantee simultaneously for all targets and distributions. A negative answer must show that for every proposed pair of universal integers \(A,k\), some finite class admits no such learner at any positive integer sample size within the proposed bound. Computational lower bounds, proper-learning obstructions that disappear for improper learners, or a result only for one fixed VC dimension do not refute the statement.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge1\), a function \(\alpha:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to[0,1]\) with \(\lim_{d\to\infty}\alpha(d)=0\), a uniform randomized mechanism \(M\), and a uniform deterministic evaluator \(E\) satisfying the following statement? For every integer \(d\ge2\), put \(n=d^{C}\). For every explicitly given database \(D\in(\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\), \(M(d,D)\) runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(n+d\), satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite binary synopsis \(S\). With probability at least \(2/3\) over \(M\)'s random bits, this one synopsis satisfies \[\left|E(d,S,J,a)-q_{J,a}(D)\right|\le\alpha(d)\] simultaneously for every \(J\subseteq[d]\) and \(a\in\{0,1\}^{J}\). The evaluator runs in worst-case time polynomial in \(d+|S|\), outputs a binary-encoded rational, and has no further access to the database. The synopsis may be arbitrary: it need not be synthetic data or describe a consistent probability distribution.
cards.definitions: \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A marginal query \((J,a)\) asks for the fraction of rows agreeing with the assignment \(a\) on the coordinates in \(J\): \[q_{J,a}(D)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1\{\forall j\in J,\ D_{ij}=a_j\}.\] All orders \(0\le|J|\le d\) are included; the empty query equals one. Each query can be encoded as a length-\(d\) word over \(\{*,0,1\}\), indicating omitted coordinates or required bits; fix any constant-length binary encoding of these symbols. Thus there are \(3^{d}\) queries with descriptions of length \(O(d)\). The database is an ordered \(n\)-by-\(d\) bit matrix. For every ordered pair of equal-size databases \(D,D'\) differing at one row and every set \(O\) of binary output strings, privacy requires \[\Pr[M(d,D)\in O]\le e\Pr[M(d,D')\in O]+1/(100n^{2}).\] It is a guarantee on the whole synopsis distribution. \(M\) and \(E\) are ordinary classical multitape Turing machines with no advice, oracle or shared private database state; \(M\) uses independent fair bits. One fixed polynomial bounds its time, output length and number of random bits on every execution. One fixed polynomial bounds the evaluator's time on every valid query and synopsis. The probability of simultaneous accuracy is required separately for every database, with no input-distribution promise. All of \(C,\alpha,M,E\) and their polynomial bounds are chosen before \(d,D\). The convergence condition means that for every real \(\eta>0\), there is \(d_0\) such that \(\alpha(d)\le\eta\) for all \(d\ge d_0\); no computable convergence rate or procedure for evaluating \(\alpha\) is required. Error is an absolute error in a row fraction in \([0,1]\), not in the unnormalized count. These are the concrete synopsis, privacy and sample-size conventions already selected for this card in September 2026; they are not claimed equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order variant of the source question.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove this existence statement or its logical negation in Lean. A positive answer must exhibit the fixed uniform machines, exponent, polynomial resource bounds and vanishing error function and prove both privacy and simultaneous accuracy on every valid database. A negative answer must exclude all such choices; hardness only under an unproved cryptographic assumption proves the corresponding conditional obstruction, not the unconditional negation. Fixed positive error, accuracy only for most queries or typical databases, a polynomial number of interactive queries, or a runtime polynomial in the exponential number of all query answers does not meet the stated criterion. The target is the existence of a vanishing-error polynomial-time synopsis, rather than a numerical value requiring additive \(1/100\) determination.
cards.why: Marginals are basic summaries of relationships among attributes. The question asks whether the large information-theoretic usefulness of private high-dimensional data can be captured by a compact, efficiently evaluated object using polynomially many records. It isolates a statistical-versus-computational gap for a concrete query family while allowing outputs more flexible than synthetic datasets.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures how often a selected pattern occurs in a set of attributes. Low-order queries concern small attribute groups; this problem includes every order. There are exponentially many queries, but each query has a short description. Polynomial running time therefore requires a reusable compact synopsis with a query evaluator, rather than an explicit table of all answers.

Privacy and accuracy concern different quantifiers. Changing one person’s entire row must leave the output distribution nearly unchanged. For each fixed database, a single successful synopsis must answer every query accurately at once. Evaluating it after release accesses no additional records. A guarantee for each query separately with a fresh failure probability would not give the requested simultaneous event.

Vadhan’s 2017 open question asks for vanishing error with polynomially many records and polynomial computation. The current card retains the previously approved approximate-privacy parameters and a noninteractive binary synopsis. The survey’s alternative question about some growing but restricted order is not substituted for the all-orders requirement.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give a subexponential per-query algorithm on small databases. Theorem 1.1 handles a sequence of adaptively chosen marginal queries at fixed absolute error and its database-size guarantee depends on the length of that sequence. This is meaningful progress, but is not a polynomial-time construction of one synopsis answering all orders with vanishing error.

The survey’s synthetic-data hardness theorem assumes one-way functions and restricts the output to a new database, even for two-way marginals. It does not rule out an arbitrary synopsis: the survey explicitly contrasts that obstruction with efficient nonsynthetic answers to low-order marginals. The benchmark deliberately retains this broader output interface.

The checked December 2025 weighted-Fourier paper provides exact optimality for weighted or maximum noise variance within Gaussian factorization mechanisms. Its runtime is polynomial in the dataset and the explicit output/workload size. For the entire \(3^{d}\)-query family that size is exponential, and variance optimality within that mechanism class is not a general polynomial-synopsis theorem or impossibility result.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.
