context_blocks.text: A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute integer \(C\geq3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph promised to be \(3\)-colourable, outputs a proper colouring using at most \(C\) colours with probability at least \(2/3\)? The same palette bound and finite program must work for all graph sizes. This card retains the explicitly adopted randomized version of the constant-palette problem.
cards.definitions:
The input is an explicit finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), with \(n\geq1\), a unary size header and an adjacency matrix. There are no loops or parallel edges; isolated vertices count toward \(n\). The binary input length \(L\) is of order \(n^2+1\). The promise asserts the existence of a proper colouring with at most three colours, but supplies no colouring or other witness.

A proper \(k\)-colouring is a function \(c:[n]\to[k]\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every edge \(\{u,v\}\). A successful output explicitly lists one binary colour index in \([C]\) for each vertex, in vertex order. The algorithm may instead output a failure symbol. A candidate can be checked against the palette bound and all edges in polynomial time; invalid candidates can be converted to failure. Successful runs must colour every vertex and leave no monochromatic edge.

Use one randomized multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(K,d\) such that every computation takes at most \(K(L+1)^d\) bit operations on every graph and every random-bit sequence. All arithmetic precision, output and random-bit generation are included. The random bits are independent and fair, there are polynomially many of them in each run, and the machine has no advice or oracle. Deterministic algorithms are included. No correctness or success-probability requirement is imposed outside the three-colourability promise, but the time bound still applies.

For every promised graph, the probability of a valid \(C\)-colouring must be at least \(2/3\), over the internal bits alone. This is a guarantee for each individual input, not an average over random graphs. The existentially chosen \(C,K,d,A\) are fixed before the graph: \(C\) cannot depend on \(n\), degree, density or the particular input. The exponent and constants may depend on the selected palette bound because only one constant palette is required. Independent repetition can amplify the success probability after checking outputs; exact recognition of the three-colourability promise is not required.

There is no planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition assumption. A palette of six, one hundred or any other fixed integer could establish a positive answer. A number of colours growing with \(n\), however slowly, does not satisfy the constant-palette requirement.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of at least one such constant \(C\) and algorithm, or a proof in Lean that no such pair exists. A positive answer must verify all-input worst-case polynomial bit complexity and, for every promised graph, success probability at least \(2/3\) with a proper colouring of the full graph using that one palette.

A negative answer must exclude every absolute \(C\geq3\) and every uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm with the stated guarantee. Unconditional NP-hardness of each three-versus-\(C\) decision promise would give a complexity-theoretic obstruction, but deducing nonexistence of these randomized algorithms from it additionally requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). An unproved separation or Label Cover hypothesis cannot be treated as established in an answer to this unconditional question. Hardness for five colours alone, fixed-point-logic inexpressibility, an algorithm with a growing palette, partial colouring, or a restricted input family does not settle the full target.

cards.status_note: The exact randomized constant-palette algorithm question remains source-open in this review. A new14September2026 preprint, Fei–Minzer–Wang ECCC TR26-179, claims in Corollary1.7 unconditional NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k decision gap. On16September2026 its introductory definitions, main theorem and exact corollary were checked; its95-page proof was not independently audited. Even if that claimed theorem is established, ruling out the randomized algorithms quantified here additionally requires NP different from RP. Thus it is important new claimed hardness evidence, not an unconditional resolution of this algorithm-existence target. Older references describing six-colour decision hardness as open are historical accounts superseded by this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.

cards.context:
The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

The algebraic PCSP theorem gives unconditional NP-hardness of the three-versus-five decision gap. A randomized five-colouring search algorithm with the guarantee in this card would yield an RP algorithm for SAT after applying the reduction and checking its output, so excluding such a randomized algorithm requires \(\mathsf{NP}\ne\mathsf{RP}\). Here RP means polynomial time with no accepting computation on a NO-instance and acceptance probability at least one half on every YES-instance. The result addresses only small fixed palettes, leaving six, one hundred and every other larger constant unexcluded by that theorem alone.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde O(n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Fixed-point logic with counting augments first-order descriptions by iterative fixed points and counting operators. On unordered graphs it does not express every polynomial-time algorithm available on an explicit binary encoding. Thus the March 2026 theorem is an unconditional limitation of a powerful logic, but a different machine using the encoding’s order is not covered.

The14September2026 Fei–Minzer–Wang preprint claims a perfectly complete4-to-1 game theorem and, in Corollary1.7, NP-hardness of every fixed three-versus-k colouring gap. Its complete proof has not been independently audited here. If established, this removes the extra Label Cover conjecture from that hardness claim, but excluding the randomized search algorithms in this card would still require NP different from RP. The distinction follows because candidate colourings are efficiently checkable, giving one-sided error after a gap reduction.

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
cards.definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance. This editorial audit does not supply a Lean formalization.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are separately decidable: plain word equations by Makanin’s theorem and integer linear arithmetic by Presburger’s theorem. Their combination constrains both letter alignment and numerical size, and neither theorem alone settles their interaction.

Length identities can omit crucial content. For distinct letters \(a,b\), the word equation \(Xa=bX\) has no finite-word solution, although its induced length equality \(|X|+1=1+|X|\) is always satisfied. This illustrates why the target concerns a common word substitution, not merely a consistent length vector.

Restrictions on counts of individual letters, full Parikh vectors or additional quantifier alternation can yield different decidability results. Those predicates do not occur in the present input language. The distinction is explicit in Ciobanu’s survey.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on their solution lengths. Quadratic means each unknown appears at most twice across the equation. Their RP 2025 paper appeared online in November 2025; its proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. This restricted theorem does not cover an arbitrary system with unrestricted variable occurrences.

The IJCAR 2026 paper gives a sufficient termination condition and a partial converse for extended Nielsen transformations. The theorem concerns a specific procedure and a graph condition on an extended equation; it does not establish that every input of the unrestricted satisfiability problem is decidable. Its full preprint explicitly retains the general open question.

The checked July 2026 preprint states NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints over two letters. Its NEXP-completeness theorem concerns existential arithmetic with divisibility. These are distinct claims, and neither is a decision procedure or an undecidability proof for the current card.

The saved target is a conjunction, while that lower-bound corollary permits disjunctions. Finite expansion relates their decidability questions, but need not preserve polynomial input size; the corollary is therefore not presented here as a checked NEXP lower bound for the exact conjunction encoding. Allowing empty substitutions is likewise kept distinct from the preprint’s nonerasing convention.

cards.title: NP membership of word-equation satisfiability
cards.formal:
Let \(\mathrm{WE}\) be the language of encodings of satisfiable word equations \(u=v\) over finite free monoids, as defined below. Is
\[
\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}?
\]
Explicitly, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine \(V\), a constant \(C\ge1\) and an integer \(k\ge1\) such that \(V\) halts on every pair of bit strings \((e,w)\) within \(C(|e|+|w|+1)^k\) steps and, for every valid equation encoding \(e\) of length \(N\),
\[
e\in\mathrm{WE}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ 
\bigl(|w|\le C(N+1)^k\ \text{and}\ V(e,w)=1\bigr)?
\]
The verifier rejects invalid equation encodings. The same machine and constants work for all alphabets, equations and variable sets.
cards.why: Word equations are a basic model of string constraints and associative unification. Their decidability is established, but the gap between NP-hardness and polynomial-space algorithms leaves the complexity of short verifiable evidence unresolved. NP membership would place the unrestricted satisfiability problem at the familiar NP-complete boundary.
cards.status_note: Ordinary word-equation satisfiability is NP-hard and decidable in nondeterministic linear space, hence in PSPACE. Saarela’s STACS 2026 introduction explicitly identifies membership in NP as open. The newer length-constraint hardness claim concerns a larger problem. The user selected NP membership and merged TCS-0171 into this card on 16 September 2026. No resolution was found in the bounded review through that date.

context_blocks.text: A variable stands for an entire finite word, not for one letter. For example, an equation can require two occurrences of the same unknown word to match material appearing at different positions on the other side. Concatenation couples the lengths and contents of all substitutions.

Makanin established decidability, and later work reduced the space needed to decide satisfiability. The 1998 RTA question predates the polynomial-space improvement, so its much larger upper bound is historical provenance rather than the current frontier.

Jeż’s 2017 theorem places satisfiability in nondeterministic linear space measured in input bits. This implies membership in PSPACE, the class decidable using polynomial working space. A space bound alone need not limit the number of computation steps to a polynomial, so it does not supply NP membership.

An explicit substitution may be much longer than the input equation. The NP question is therefore about succinct evidence that can be checked quickly, not about requiring a short fully expanded solution. Existing work on compressed solutions explains this distinction, but the card does not mandate any particular evidence format.

Saarela’s 2026 theorem simplifies parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. Its introduction still lists NP membership for general word equations as open. A result about the structure of that restricted solution set does not settle the unrestricted decision problem.

The June 2026 preprint claims stronger hardness for formulas that combine word equations with length constraints. Those extra arithmetic constraints change the input language. The claim therefore does not establish a lower bound excluding NP for plain equations, and its full proof was not independently audited in this review.

The earlier two atlas records used different historical names for overlapping complexity questions. This card is now the single active NP-membership target. The duplicate’s source and provenance remain available, while the broader request for an exact complexity classification is no longer the benchmark question.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(a\ge1\), the constant alphabet is \(\Sigma=\{a_1,\ldots,a_a\}\). Its free monoid \(\Sigma^*\) is the set of finite words, including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as the operation. Concatenation is associative and \(\varepsilon\) is its identity; distinct letters do not commute by assumption.

The variable set is \(\mathcal X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_r\}\), disjoint from \(\Sigma\), where \(r\ge0\). An equation is a pair \(u,v\in(\Sigma\cup\mathcal X)^*\). Both sides are explicitly written token sequences. A solution assigns one word \(\sigma(X_i)\in\Sigma^*\) to each variable, fixes every constant letter, and extends by concatenation. The equation is satisfiable exactly when \(\sigma(u)=\sigma(v)\) for some assignment. All occurrences of a variable receive the same word. Empty words, repeated variables, variables on both sides, and equations with empty sides are allowed. There are no length constraints, regular-language restrictions, inverse symbols or inequalities.

One precise binary encoding is as follows. Write \(1^a0\,1^r0\,1^{\ell_u}0\,1^{\ell_v}0\), where \(\ell_u=|u|\) and \(\ell_v=|v|\) count tokens. Follow this header by all tokens of \(u\) and then all tokens of \(v\). Each token is encoded in \(b=\lceil\log_2(a+r+1)\rceil\) bits: code \(i\) for \(a_i\) and code \(a+j\) for \(X_j\). Codes outside \(1,\ldots,a+r\) are invalid. There must be exactly \(\ell_u+\ell_v\) token blocks and no trailing data. Thus
\[
N=a+r+\ell_u+\ell_v+4+b(\ell_u+\ell_v).
\]
This explicit encoding fixes bit complexity without allowing compressed input equations.

\(\mathrm{NP}\) is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates accepted by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier, with precisely the soundness and completeness quantified above. A certificate is any finite binary string. It need not contain the substituted words explicitly, and no particular compressed representation is prescribed. A satisfiable input must have some short accepting certificate; an unsatisfiable input must have none.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of \(\mathrm{WE}\in\mathrm{NP}\). A positive answer must specify the verifier and prove the polynomial time and certificate bounds together with soundness and completeness for every input. A negative answer must prove that no such verifier exists; failure of one certificate format or long explicit solutions is insufficient. This binary target has no numerical \(1/100\) tolerance. Results only for boundedly many variables, bounded occurrences, or added constraints do not decide the full statement.

cards.context:
A variable stands for an entire finite word, not for one letter. For example, an equation can require two occurrences of the same unknown word to match material appearing at different positions on the other side. Concatenation couples the lengths and contents of all substitutions.

Makanin established decidability, and later work reduced the space needed to decide satisfiability. The 1998 RTA question predates the polynomial-space improvement, so its much larger upper bound is historical provenance rather than the current frontier.

Jeż’s 2017 theorem places satisfiability in nondeterministic linear space measured in input bits. This implies membership in PSPACE, the class decidable using polynomial working space. A space bound alone need not limit the number of computation steps to a polynomial, so it does not supply NP membership.

An explicit substitution may be much longer than the input equation. The NP question is therefore about succinct evidence that can be checked quickly, not about requiring a short fully expanded solution. Existing work on compressed solutions explains this distinction, but the card does not mandate any particular evidence format.

Saarela’s 2026 theorem simplifies parametric descriptions for constant-free equations on three variables. Its introduction still lists NP membership for general word equations as open. A result about the structure of that restricted solution set does not settle the unrestricted decision problem.

The June 2026 preprint claims stronger hardness for formulas that combine word equations with length constraints. Those extra arithmetic constraints change the input language. The claim therefore does not establish a lower bound excluding NP for plain equations, and its full proof was not independently audited in this review.

The earlier two atlas records used different historical names for overlapping complexity questions. This card is now the single active NP-membership target. The duplicate’s source and provenance remain available, while the broader request for an exact complexity classification is no longer the benchmark question.

cards.definitions: A finite relational vocabulary \(\tau\) lists finitely many relation symbols with fixed positive arities. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A has a nonempty finite domain and interprets each r-ary symbol as a subset of \(A^{r}\). An isomorphism is a bijection between domains that preserves and reflects every relation. For computation, label the n domain elements by \([n]\) and encode the domain explicitly together with all relation tables in binary. Different labelings of the same abstract structure are permitted; the input supplies no distinguished order relation. A Boolean property is an isomorphism-closed class of structures of one vocabulary. It is in PTIME when one deterministic Turing machine decides membership for every encoding in time polynomial in its length. The logic has a decidable set of finite binary sentence encodings with their vocabularies. Each sentence \(\varphi\) has a truth value \(A\models \varphi\) invariant under isomorphism. One total computable compiler, given a valid \((\tau ,\varphi )\), outputs a deterministic machine \(M_{\varphi}\) and integers \(C_{\varphi},k_{\varphi}\ge 1\) such that \(M_{\varphi}\) decides \(A\models \varphi\) in at most \(C_{\varphi}(N+1)^{k_{\varphi}}\) steps on every valid input structure encoding of length N. Finally, for every finite \(\tau\) and every PTIME Boolean property Q of \(\tau\)-structures, some fixed \(\tau\)-sentence \(\varphi\) satisfies \(A\models \varphi\) exactly when \(A\in Q\) for all finite A. Neither sentence construction from an arbitrary machine nor polynomial-time compilation is required. The exponent may depend on the sentence. No uniform polynomial bound for the combined input \((\varphi ,A)\) is imposed. The same syntax and compiler must work across vocabularies; no oracle, advice or externally chosen ordering is supplied to the semantics.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution gives a formalism satisfying decidable syntax, invariant semantics, effective polynomial-time compilation and expressive completeness for every finite relational vocabulary. A negative resolution proves that no formalism can satisfy all these requirements. Failure of one named logic, capture on a restricted class of structures, or capture with an additional input order does not decide general existence.

context_blocks.title: Properties should survive renaming
context_blocks.text: A graph with vertices called 1, 2 and 3 has the same abstract edges after a consistent permutation of those names. The property “the graph is connected” is unchanged; the property “vertex 1 has a neighbour named 2” can change. A logic for structures must express the first kind of property. An ordinary algorithm still receives a labeled encoding and may use its order internally, but its final Boolean answer must depend only on the structure being represented.

context_blocks.title: Why an effective syntax matters
context_blocks.text: One could assign a symbol to each polynomial-time property and declare that the symbol names that property. This supplies no way to evaluate the symbols. The compiler requirement makes the connection operational: from a sentence, one must obtain an actual algorithm and its polynomial clock. Similarly, listing all clocked machines does not ensure that every listed machine gives the same answer after relabeling its input. The task is to combine effective enumeration with invariance and full expressive power.

context_blocks.title: The known ordered theorem
context_blocks.text: The Immerman–Vardi theorem captures polynomial time by fixed-point logic on structures equipped with a linear order. Fixed-point operators express iterative constructions such as repeatedly extending a reachability relation until no new pairs appear. The order allows the logic to organize elements and simulate an ordinary computation. In the present question the order is absent from the mathematical input. Adding one to every structure changes what the sentence is permitted to access, so the ordered theorem does not directly settle the unordered case.

context_blocks.title: Capturing is not one universal time bound
context_blocks.text: One sentence may compile to a quadratic algorithm and another to an algorithm taking the tenth power of the input size. Both are permitted. The sentence is fixed when its data complexity is measured. Conversely, expressive completeness asks for a single sentence for an entire property on all finite input sizes. Writing a separate sentence for each graph, or a different sentence for each domain size, would not supply the required description.

context_blocks.title: The remaining gap
context_blocks.text: Known extensions of fixed-point logic add counting, linear algebra or symmetry-preserving computation, but ruling out a particular candidate is not a proof that no logic exists. Lichter and Schweitzer’s witnessed symmetric choice extends a candidate logic and yields capturing results on classes where isomorphism is definable; the premise is not known for all structures. Dahan’s August 2026 paper explicitly retains the general question. Its obstruction to choosing small symmetric generating sets concerns a structured output task, rather than proving that no logic can express every PTIME Boolean property. Finally, if \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), existential second-order logic would capture P by Fagin’s theorem and would have effective polynomial-time evaluation. Thus a proof that no such logic exists would also separate P from NP.

sentences: Is there an effective logic for all polynomial-time properties of finite unordered structures?

cards.title: FO model checking on hereditary monadically dependent graph classes
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal:
For every hereditary effectively monadically dependent class \(\mathcal C\) of finite simple undirected graphs, is first-order model checking fixed-parameter tractable with a computable parameter dependence?

Precisely, does every such \(\mathcal C\) admit a single deterministic algorithm \(A_{\mathcal C}\), a total computable function \(f_{\mathcal C}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and a constant integer \(d_{\mathcal C}\ge0\) such that, for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every first-order graph sentence \(\varphi\), the algorithm outputs whether \(G\models\varphi\) within
\[f_{\mathcal C}(|\varphi|)\,(|V(G)|+1)^{d_{\mathcal C}}\]
steps? The algorithm receives only the graph and the sentence, in the encodings below, and must halt on every input. The exponent may depend on the class but not on the sentence. The effective structural hypothesis is the computable powerset-obstruction bound defined below.
cards.definitions:
Graph class and promise. A finite simple undirected graph has a finite vertex set and a symmetric irreflexive adjacency relation \(E\); the empty graph is permitted. A class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under graph isomorphism. It is hereditary if \(G[S]\in\mathcal C\) for every \(G\in\mathcal C\) and every \(S\subseteq V(G)\), where \(G[S]\) retains exactly the edges with both endpoints in \(S\). The class is fixed before the algorithm is chosen, not given as part of an instance. No decision procedure for membership in the class is assumed. Correctness and the displayed time bound are required only when the input graph belongs to the class. On other inputs the algorithm may return either answer, but must halt.

First-order syntax and truth. The graph signature has equality and a binary adjacency symbol, with variables \(x_i\) indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\). Formulas are built from atoms \(x_i=x_j\), \(E(x_i,x_j)\), negation, binary conjunction, and existential quantification \(\exists x_i\); other connectives and universal quantification are abbreviations expanded into this syntax. A sentence has no free variables. Atoms are interpreted using actual equality and graph adjacency; Boolean operations have their usual truth tables, and quantifiers range over all vertices. On the empty graph an existential statement is false and a universal statement is true. The query language has no unary predicates, vertex order, arithmetic, function symbols or set quantification. Write \(G\models\varphi\) for truth of the sentence.

Encoding and computation. For a nonnegative integer \(i\), let \(\ell\) be the binary length of \(i+1\), and encode it as \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), where the last part has exactly \(\ell\) bits. Encode \(G\) with labeled vertex set \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) as \(U(n)\) followed by its upper-triangular adjacency bits, in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\). All these bits are supplied explicitly. Formulas use prefix syntax: tags 000, 001, 010, 011, 100 respectively stand for equality, adjacency, negation, conjunction and existential quantification. An atom tag is followed by \(U(i)U(j)\), negation by one encoded subformula, conjunction by two in order, and the existential tag by \(U(i)\) and one subformula. The parameter \(|\varphi|\) is this binary length, including variable indices. A valid input concatenates the graph code and one sentence code; invalid inputs may be rejected. An algorithm is a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite tape alphabet and no oracle, advice or randomness; time counts its transitions. Polynomial simulation overhead between the usual explicit graph representations and finite-word computational models can be absorbed in the class-dependent exponent and parameter function.

Unary expansions for the structural condition. For this purpose only, allow additional unary symbols \(P_j\), \(j\in\mathbb N\), with atom \(P_j(x_i)\) encoded by tag 101 followed by \(U(j)U(i)\). Each formula uses finitely many such symbols. They are interpreted independently as arbitrary vertex subsets; they may overlap. Their names and variable indices are included in formula length. There are no additional parameters or constant symbols.

Transduction. Let \(\theta(x_0,x_1)\) be any formula in this expanded syntax whose only possible free variables are \(x_0,x_1\). Given \(G\), choose arbitrary interpretations of all unary symbols used in \(\theta\). On the same vertex set, form an undirected graph by putting an edge between distinct \(u,v\) exactly when \(\theta(u,v)\lor\theta(v,u)\) holds in that expansion of \(G\). Finally keep any subset of vertices and take the induced graph on it. Denote by \(T_\theta(G)\) the set of all graphs obtainable in this way, up to isomorphism. Colors are discarded in the output. There is no copying of vertices or tuple-valued output domain in this definition.

Monadic dependence and its effective version. A class is monadically dependent when no single formula \(\theta\) produces every finite simple graph among the outputs \(T_\theta(G)\) as \(G\) ranges over the class. To state the quantitative promise, for an integer \(s\ge1\) let \(P_s\) be the bipartite powerset graph with disjoint vertex sets \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_s\}\) and \(\{b_S:S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,s\}\}\), and edges exactly \(a_i b_S\) with \(i\in S\). It has \(s+2^s\) vertices and no edges within either part.

The class \(\mathcal C\) is effectively monadically dependent if there is a total computable function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) such that
\[\forall\theta\ \forall G\in\mathcal C:\quad P_{b(|\theta|)}\notin T_\theta(G).\]
Absence means that no choice of unary predicates and retained vertex subset yields a graph isomorphic to that powerset graph. The bound is uniform over all formulas of the given length, all graphs in the class, and all their colorings. It is the effective dependence-function convention of Mählmann’s Definition 12.24, which in particular implies monadic dependence. The finite program computing \(b\) may depend on \(\mathcal C\).

Uniformity of the requested algorithm. For each class, one finite program \(A_{\mathcal C}\) must handle all input sentence lengths. It may depend on the class and its effective dependence witness, but receives neither a class-membership certificate nor a graph decomposition on an instance. The quantifiers are class-wise existence of the algorithm, computable function and exponent; no single procedure that accepts arbitrary descriptions of classes and constructs their algorithms is required. There is no prescribed growth rate for \(f_{\mathcal C}\), beyond total computability.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish, for every class satisfying the hereditary and effective-dependence promises, one total deterministic algorithm and one computable parameter bound with a sentence-independent polynomial exponent, for the specified graph-and-sentence input model.

A negative answer must establish a particular hereditary effectively monadically dependent class for which no such algorithm, computable parameter function and fixed exponent work. In particular, every candidate total deterministic algorithm and bound must fail on some graph in that class and some sentence, either in correctness or in running time. An obstruction applying only to one proposed algorithm, an ineffective class, or a restricted decomposition method is insufficient. A conditional hardness result alone does not refute this unconditional target unless its additional assumption is also proved. Structural existence theorems, a different algorithm for each sentence length, randomized algorithms, or algorithms supplied with extra decompositions do not by themselves meet the criterion.
cards.why: First-order formulas express a broad family of graph queries, but direct evaluation lets the graph-size exponent grow with the query. The proposed structural condition aims to explain when that dependence can be confined to a computable function of the query alone, even on dense graph classes. Settling this tractability direction would complement the established hardness of hereditary classes that can logically encode arbitrary graphs.

context_blocks.text: First-order model checking asks whether a finite graph satisfies an input sentence. Clique, independent-set and dominating-set queries of a specified size are basic examples. Trying all assignments of vertices to variables gives polynomial time for each fixed sentence, but its exponent depends on the sentence. Fixed-parameter tractability requires one exponent for all sentences on the chosen class.

For example, a sentence can assert the existence of a fixed number of vertices such that every other vertex is adjacent to at least one of them. Increasing that number increases the sentence length and the direct enumeration cost. The target permits an arbitrarily large computable cost depending on sentence length, while keeping a fixed polynomial dependence on the graph size. It is a uniform guarantee across the whole query language.

The hereditary condition is closure under deleting vertices, keeping all remaining edges. It allows sparse and dense classes alike. Complete graphs illustrate why edge density is not itself the barrier: a dense class may still have tightly controlled logical behavior. The conjectured boundary uses what a fixed formula can encode after arbitrary unary marking, rather than an edge-count bound.

A transduction changes the edge relation according to a formula, after vertices have been marked by finitely many unary predicates, and may discard vertices. The formula is fixed while graph size grows. Monadic independence means that one such fixed scheme can yield every finite graph. Dependence excludes this unrestricted encoding, while allowing richer structure than monadic stability.

Computability is a genuine qualification in the saved target. A class can have a finite obstruction bound at each formula length without any computable function dominating those bounds. The dissertation illustrates this distinction with graph classes indexed by Busy Beaver growth. That example shows why a proof with arbitrary class-dependent constants cannot automatically be advertised as a computable FPT bound; it is not itself an unconditional counterexample to the present effective conjecture.

The structural witness and the query algorithm play different roles. The function b bounds powerset graphs obtainable by all short colored formulas; it does not recognize which graphs belong to the class. The requested algorithm receives a promised member of the class and an uncolored sentence. Neither a membership test nor a decomposition oracle is included in the input.

Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that model checking is \(\mathrm{AW}[*]\)-hard on every hereditary monadically independent class. Their stronger interpretation theorem produces uncolored instances efficiently, so this is not merely a hardness statement with extra vertex colors supplied. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{AW}[*]\), the independent side cannot have FPT model checking. That conditional intractability does not prove the positive dependent side.

Monadic stability is the stronger condition excluding arbitrarily large half-graphs under transductions: a half-graph of order \(s\) has two disjoint parts \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\), with edge \(a_i b_j\) exactly when \(i\le j\). The stable-class model-checking theorem gives a major positive case. The dissertation makes its parameter function computable under effective stability bounds; ordinary stability alone should not silently be substituted for that effective hypothesis.

Merge-width measures graph construction sequences that merge vertex groups and resolve pairs as edges or nonedges. At radius r, the width bounds how many current groups a vertex can reach using at most r resolved pairs. The existing bounded-merge-width model-checking theorem assumes that a witnessing sequence is supplied. Existence of a useful sequence alone does not meet the card’s input model.

The July 2026 paper proves almost linear neighborhood complexity for every monadically dependent class. Writing \(N_G(v)\) for the neighbors of \(v\), for every \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}\) such that for all \(G\in\mathcal C\) and all nonempty \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the number of distinct sets \(N_G(v)\cap S\) is at most \(c_{\mathcal C,\eta}|S|^{1+\eta}\). The nonempty-set qualification avoids the zero-size edge case.

The same paper constructs radius-one merge-width sequences in \(O(n^5)\) time, with width \(n^{o(1)}\) on every monadically dependent class. Here \(n^{o(1)}\) means that for every fixed positive exponent the width is eventually at most a constant times that power of \(n\), with constants depending on the class. Dreier and Kuske’s February 2026 work speeds up low-crossing orders and neighborhood covers, with a faster model-checking application for monadically stable classes. Its ordering and cover subroutines use randomness. A faster theorem on that already understood subclass does not establish the deterministic guarantee for every effectively monadically dependent class.

The July 2026 paper explicitly retains the general tractability direction as open. A positive answer here would establish the effective algorithmic direction of the proposed classification. A negative answer would require an effective hereditary class that defeats every single uniform algorithm with computable parameter dependence, not merely a class whose currently known decomposition bounds are ineffective.

cards.context:
First-order model checking asks whether a finite graph satisfies an input sentence. Clique, independent-set and dominating-set queries of a specified size are basic examples. Trying all assignments of vertices to variables gives polynomial time for each fixed sentence, but its exponent depends on the sentence. Fixed-parameter tractability requires one exponent for all sentences on the chosen class.

For example, a sentence can assert the existence of a fixed number of vertices such that every other vertex is adjacent to at least one of them. Increasing that number increases the sentence length and the direct enumeration cost. The target permits an arbitrarily large computable cost depending on sentence length, while keeping a fixed polynomial dependence on the graph size. It is a uniform guarantee across the whole query language.

The hereditary condition is closure under deleting vertices, keeping all remaining edges. It allows sparse and dense classes alike. Complete graphs illustrate why edge density is not itself the barrier: a dense class may still have tightly controlled logical behavior. The conjectured boundary uses what a fixed formula can encode after arbitrary unary marking, rather than an edge-count bound.

A transduction changes the edge relation according to a formula, after vertices have been marked by finitely many unary predicates, and may discard vertices. The formula is fixed while graph size grows. Monadic independence means that one such fixed scheme can yield every finite graph. Dependence excludes this unrestricted encoding, while allowing richer structure than monadic stability.

Computability is a genuine qualification in the saved target. A class can have a finite obstruction bound at each formula length without any computable function dominating those bounds. The dissertation illustrates this distinction with graph classes indexed by Busy Beaver growth. That example shows why a proof with arbitrary class-dependent constants cannot automatically be advertised as a computable FPT bound; it is not itself an unconditional counterexample to the present effective conjecture.

The structural witness and the query algorithm play different roles. The function b bounds powerset graphs obtainable by all short colored formulas; it does not recognize which graphs belong to the class. The requested algorithm receives a promised member of the class and an uncolored sentence. Neither a membership test nor a decomposition oracle is included in the input.

Dreier, Mählmann and Toruńczyk prove that model checking is \(\mathrm{AW}[*]\)-hard on every hereditary monadically independent class. Their stronger interpretation theorem produces uncolored instances efficiently, so this is not merely a hardness statement with extra vertex colors supplied. Under the standard assumption \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne\mathrm{AW}[*]\), the independent side cannot have FPT model checking. That conditional intractability does not prove the positive dependent side.

Monadic stability is the stronger condition excluding arbitrarily large half-graphs under transductions: a half-graph of order \(s\) has two disjoint parts \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\), with edge \(a_i b_j\) exactly when \(i\le j\). The dissertation makes its parameter function computable under effective stability bounds; ordinary stability alone should not silently be substituted for that effective hypothesis.

cards.title: Sunflower conjecture
cards.formal:
For every integer \(r\ge3\), does there exist a real constant \(C_r\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite set \(X\), and every family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\{S\subseteq X:|S|=k\}\),
\[
|\mathcal F|>C_r^k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists\text{ distinct }S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal F\ \exists K\subseteq X\ \forall i\ne j:\ S_i\cap S_j=K?
\]
The constant may depend on \(r\) but not on the set size \(k\), the ground set or the family. The conclusion is the existence of an ordinary \(r\)-sunflower.
cards.definitions:
A family here is a finite set of subsets, so identical members are not repeated. It is \(k\)-uniform when every member has exactly \(k\) elements. There is no bound on the finite ground-set size \(|X|\). An \(r\)-sunflower consists of \(r\) pairwise distinct members whose pairwise intersections are all the same set \(K\), called the core. For \(r\ge3\), this core also equals the intersection of all selected members. Removing \(K\) leaves pairwise disjoint petals. The core may be empty, in which case the selected sets are pairwise disjoint. For distinct equal-sized members their petals are nonempty.

The quantifier order is \(\forall r\,\exists C_r\,\forall k,X,\mathcal F\). No single base independent of \(r\) is requested. One may equivalently require an integer \(C_r\ge2\), since a larger integer base preserves the upper bound. An eventual bound for all sufficiently large \(k\), with the threshold depending on \(r\), also yields the displayed all-\(k\) formulation by enlarging \(C_r\) to cover finitely many small sizes.

The classical sunflower lemma bounds the size of any sunflower-free \(k\)-uniform family by \(k!(r-1)^k\), independently of its ground set. Consequently the largest such size \(S_r(k)\) exists as a finite integer, even though the ground set is unrestricted. The conjecture is equivalently \(S_r(k)\le C_r^k\) for all \(k\). It does not ask for the exact value, a numerical estimate or constant-factor asymptotics of \(S_r(k)\).

The source also states the conjecture for sets of size at most \(k\). Padding every smaller set to size \(k\) with fresh elements unique to that member preserves pairwise intersections and reduces that variant to the displayed one. This observation is not a claim about robust sunflowers: their probabilistic coverage requirement is stronger, and lower bounds for that stronger structure do not refute the ordinary conjecture.

There is no computational requirement on finding the sunflower or computing the constants. This is a quantified extremal-combinatorial proposition, so the numerical absolute-error convention does not replace it.

context_blocks.text: The classical lemma forces a sunflower only after a factorial-sized threshold. The conjecture would replace this by an exponential whose base is independent of the set size.

Modern bounds remove most of the classical growth but still have a base growing logarithmically with the set size. The robust sunflower method has its own obstruction at that scale, which does not settle ordinary sunflowers.
Sunflower structure supports computational lower bounds and other combinatorial reductions. A uniform exponential threshold would strengthen the general principle used in such applications.

cards.why: A general combinatorial principle with established applications to computational lower bounds and parameterized reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed conjecture or its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite base for every fixed \(r\ge3\). A negative proof must supply one fixed \(r\ge3\) for which every candidate base \(C\ge1\) admits a \(k\)-uniform family of more than \(C^k\) members with no \(r\)-sunflower. Improving known superconstant bases, proving only the case of one petal count, or disproving a robust-sunflower variant does not decide the full statement.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A partial order \(\le_P\) is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive binary relation on \([n]\). Distinct elements \(x,y\) are incomparable if neither \(x\le_P y\) nor \(y\le_P x\); a total order has no incomparable pair. A linear extension is a bijection \(L:[n]\to[n]\) such that \(L(a)<L(b)\) whenever \(a\le_P b\) and \(a\ne b\). Let \(E(P)\) be the finite nonempty set of all linear extensions, \(e(P)=|E(P)|\), and \(e_P(x,y)=|\{L\in E(P):L(x)<L(y)\}|\). Probabilities use the uniform distribution on the entire set \(E(P)\), so \(\Pr[L(x)<L(y)]=e_P(x,y)/e(P)\). The endpoints \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) are included. The pair may depend on the full finite order; there is no algorithmic or representation restriction. In the context, width is the largest size of a set of pairwise incomparable elements, height the largest size of a totally ordered subset, and the cover graph joins \(x,y\) if one is strictly below the other with no element strictly between them. The balance constant is \(\beta(P)=\max_{x\ne y}\min\{e_P(x,y),e_P(y,x)\}/e(P)\).

context_blocks.text: A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.

cards.context:
A partial order records comparisons already known, and its linear extensions are all complete rankings still compatible with that information. The conjecture says that unless only one ranking remains, some unresolved comparison splits these possible rankings into two substantial groups. Neither outcome may leave more than two thirds of them. The distribution is uniform over whole rankings, not over the currently available choices in a stepwise topological sort.

Take three elements with \(a<b\) and c unrelated to both. The three linear extensions are abc, acb and cab. The probability that a precedes c is \(2/3\), while the probability that b precedes c is \(1/3\). No incomparable pair is closer to a half. This small example shows that the universal interval cannot be narrowed to \([1/3+\eta ,2/3- \eta ]\) for any \(\eta >0\). In a total order every pair instead has probability zero or one, which explains the excluded case.

Uniform local choices need not produce uniform extensions. In the same example, choosing randomly between the two initially minimal elements a and c gives cab probability \(1/2\), and gives abc and acb probability \(1/4\) each. Those are different from the required probabilities \(1/3\) each. Fixing the probability space prevents a superficially similar random-ordering question from replacing the conjecture.

Brightwell, Felsner and Trotter prove the weaker universal bound \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\ge (5- \sqrt{5})/10\approx 0.2764\). It already guarantees an informative comparison and improves the earlier \(3/11\) bound of Kahn and Saks. The requested value \(1/3\) is a sharper extremal constant, rather than the first guarantee of any fixed positive balance.

The conjecture is known for substantial classes, including width-two and height-two orders, and orders whose cover graph is a forest. Width limits how many elements can be mutually incomparable; height limits the length of a chain. These are distinct restrictions, and neither covers arbitrary finite orders. The Chan–Pak survey states the general question separately from this collection of positive cases.

Aires and Kahn obtain stronger asymptotic balance under size hypotheses: for example \(\beta (\mathrm{P})\) tends to \(1/2\) when width is at least a fixed positive fraction of the number of elements. Their 2025 paper still states the unrestricted \(1/3\)–\(2/3\) bound as a conjecture. A result for a sequence of sufficiently wide orders leaves narrower and exceptional finite orders uncovered.

Gupta’s July 2026 revision reports an exhaustive verification of the stronger Gold Partition property through fourteen elements, implying the balance conjecture for those sizes. Its arithmetic and archived artifacts are described in the paper; this review did not rerun the census. A verified finite range, however large its enumeration, does not establish the universal statement.
